item.title: What a /24 subnet actually means (and how to plan yours)
item.description: The /24 after an address says which part names the network and which part names the device. Here is what that means in practice, why one flat /24 is the trap, and how the books plan one /24 per zone with a static route and a firewall between them.
item.content:encoded:
Every example network in the books is written the same way: 192.168.10.0/24 for the house LAN, 10.30.0.0/24 for servers, 192.168.30.0/24 for IoT. That little /24 shows up on firewall interfaces, container network settings and VPN configs, and once you can read it, a lot of homelab networking stops being magic.

What the /24 tells you

An address like 192.168.30.57/24 has two parts. With a /24, the first three numbers (192.168.30) name the network, and the last number (.57) names the device on that network. Every device whose address starts with 192.168.30 is on the same subnet. A device at 192.168.10.57 is on a different one, even though it ends in the same number.

That split decides who can talk to whom:

  • Devices on the same subnet reach each other directly. On a flat home network, every device can see every other device's open ports.
  • Devices on different subnets need something to route between them, which is exactly where a firewall can sit and decide what is allowed.
  • Some traffic never crosses at all. A router does not forward multicast between subnets, which is why a phone on one network asking "is there a TV here?" never reaches a TV on another, and the cast button stays grey. Nothing is blocked; the question just never arrives.

The same notation appears on the gateway itself. When the firewall's interface is set to 192.168.30.1/24, that one line says both "my address is .1" and "everything in 192.168.30.x is on this interface".

The trap: one /24 for everything

The usual home network has one subnet behind the router. Your laptop, the smart plug, the TV, a visiting friend's phone and the Proxmox host all get an address from the same pool. The only firewall rule that matters is the one between the house and the internet: the front door is guarded while every interior door stands open.

That holds until something on the inside goes bad. Cheap smart-home gear often runs old software that rarely sees an update, a phone picks up a malicious app, a guest's laptop arrives already infected. On a flat /24, any of them can scan the subnet and find the Proxmox web interface, the NAS share or the printer with its default password.

The fix: one /24 per zone

Lock Down Your Home Network groups devices into five zones, each with its own VLAN and its own /24:

ZoneVLANSubnetFirewallDHCP range
Trusted10192.168.10.0/24.1.100 to .199
Servers20192.168.20.0/24.1static only
IoT30192.168.30.0/24.1.100 to .249
Guest40192.168.40.0/24.1.100 to .249
Management99192.168.99.0/24.1static only

Two conventions make this plan easy to live with:

  • The third number matches the VLAN ID. When you see 192.168.30.57 in a log, you know it is an IoT device without looking anything up.
  • The firewall is always .1. Every zone's gateway is the same last number, so there is nothing to remember per network.

In OPNsense, each VLAN becomes its own interface with a static address and the right prefix, for example 192.168.30.1/24. A new interface allows nothing by default: OPNsense blocks traffic arriving on an interface with no pass rules, so each new network stays dark until you write its rules. That is the right starting point.

Resist making more zones on day one. Every zone is another rule set to write, test and keep tidy; add a sixth only when you can name the rule that would be different for it.

Smaller version: a servers /24 behind OPNsense

If you are not ready for VLANs yet, Homelab the Right Way starts with a single separate network for your servers, 10.30.0.0/24, on a Linux bridge on the Proxmox host. Add the bridge in /etc/network/interfaces and apply it with ifreload -a:

auto vmbr1
iface vmbr1 inet manual
    bridge-ports none
    bridge-stp off
    bridge-fd 0

Give the OPNsense VM a NIC on vmbr1 and assign it as SERVERS with the static address 10.30.0.1/24. Static IPs are recommended for servers, so they have predictable addresses. Then move one container at a time, giving it an address inside the new /24 and OPNsense as its gateway:

pct set 120 --net0 name=eth0,bridge=vmbr1,ip=10.30.0.20/24,gw=10.30.0.1
pct exec 120 -- sh -c 'ip route; ping -c2 10.30.0.1'

Notice that ip=10.30.0.20/24 carries the /24 too: it tells the container which addresses are local and which must go through the gateway.

Before you begin, write a table of old IP to new IP, and either keep the old address as a secondary for a while or update DNS and reverse proxy entries in the same sitting.

Don't forget the route back

A new subnet is invisible to the rest of the house until something knows how to reach it. Clients on the house LAN need a route to 10.30.0.0/24. The clean way is a static route on the house router: 10.30.0.0/24 via 192.168.10.2, the OPNsense WAN address. Then allow the house LAN in on OPNsense's WAN interface for the specific ports you need, and disable Block private networks on WAN, since in this layout your "WAN" is itself a private network.

Keep your management path where it is: leave the Proxmox web UI and SSH reachable on the house LAN, so a firewall mistake never locks you out of the host.

Checklist: planning your /24s

  • You can read any address in your logs and say which network it belongs to
  • Every device is listed with the zone it belongs in
  • One VLAN ID and one /24 per zone, with the third number matching the VLAN ID
  • The firewall is .1 on every network, set with the right prefix (e.g. 192.168.30.1/24)
  • Servers use static addresses; DHCP ranges are set only where a zone needs them
  • An old IP to new IP table is written before anything moves
  • The house router has a static route to the servers subnet
  • The Proxmox web UI and SSH stay reachable on the house LAN

item.content:encoded:

This is the running list behind our product Shorts and TikToks: tech that keeps going viral AND has kept selling well for years, filtered for a homelab, desk-setup and smart-home audience. Each one got its own short video with a fictional AI presenter (the presenter is AI-generated; we do not claim to have personally tested these). No prices or ratings here because they change weekly; check the listing.

1. TP-Link TL-SG105 5-port gigabit switch

The first upgrade almost every homelab makes: one cable from the router gives you four more full-speed gigabit ports for the server, NAS, Pi and desktop. Metal case, fanless, nothing to configure. See it on Amazon

2. SanDisk 2TB Extreme Portable SSD

A pocket solid-state drive with no moving parts, USB-C, rated for drops and splashes, fast enough that a full laptop or VM backup takes minutes. See it on Amazon

3. INIU 10,000 mAh 45W power bank

Jacket-pocket size, 45 W over USB-C (enough for a USB-C laptop, tablet or Steam Deck), a short built-in detachable cable plus a USB-A port, flight-safe capacity. See it on Amazon

4. Kasa Smart Plug Ultra Mini EP10 (2-pack)

A Wi-Fi plug with no hub and no subscription: hard-reboot a frozen mini PC or router from your phone, schedule desk lights, works with Alexa, Google Home and Home Assistant. See it on Amazon

5. Alex Tech 10 ft split cable sleeve

Braided split tubing you push the cables into: ten seconds to a clean bundle behind a desk or under a rack shelf, cut to length, reusable, keeps pets off the cords. See it on Amazon

6. KAMRUI AK1PLUS mini PC (Intel N5095, 16 GB)

A palm-size, low-power desktop that is a popular first Proxmox or Home Assistant box: dual HDMI, 16 GB RAM, an M.2 SSD you can swap, and it sips power on a shelf 24/7. See it on Amazon

7. TP-Link Archer AX21 AX1800 Wi-Fi 6 router

The budget Wi-Fi 6 router that shows up in every "what router should I buy" thread: dual-band, gigabit ports, OneMesh, and it runs as a plain access point behind an OPNsense box. See it on Amazon

8. Anker 8-in-1 USB-C docking station

One cable from the laptop to two monitors, Ethernet, USB-A ports and power delivery; the desk dock people keep recommending for hybrid work setups. See it on Amazon

9. Govee 16.4 ft RGBIC LED strip

The strip behind half the desk and rack photos online: segment colours, app and voice control, music sync, and it is the Govee line Home Assistant users pick. See it on Amazon

10. Anker 2100J surge-protector power strip

A flat-plug surge protector with a 2100-joule rating, multiple outlets and USB ports: the strip to put under a desk full of chargers and small boxes. See it on Amazon

How we pick

A product makes this list when it sits near the top of its Amazon Best Sellers category, has a long record of reviews over several years, and is the kind of thing people in the homelab and desk-setup corners of YouTube, TikTok and Reddit keep making videos about. The list is refreshed as new videos go up; the newest picks are at the top of the channel's Shorts.

item.title: TP-Link TL-SG105: the 5-port gigabit switch most homelabs start with
item.description: What the TP-Link TL-SG105 unmanaged 5-port gigabit switch does, where it fits in a homelab, and what it does not do. With the short video and the Amazon link.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The Amazon link on this page supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

Get it on Amazon: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-Port Gigabit Switch

The short video on this page uses a fictional AI-generated presenter (AI face, voice and lip-sync). We have not personally tested this switch; the details below come from TP-Link's own product information. No price or rating is quoted because both change; check the listing.

The problem it solves

Most home routers have four Ethernet ports on the back. A homelab fills them fast: a server or mini PC, a NAS, a Raspberry Pi, a desktop. A small unmanaged switch fixes that with one cable: plug one of its ports into the router and the other four become extra wired ports on the same network.

What it is

  • 5 gigabit Ethernet ports (10/100/1000 Mbps, auto-negotiation on every port)
  • Metal case, no fan, so it is silent
  • Unmanaged and plug-and-play: no app, no web page, nothing to configure
  • Energy-efficient design, which matters for a box that runs 24/7 on a shelf
  • Sits on a desk or mounts on a wall
  • Works behind any router, including an OPNsense or pfSense box

Where it fits in a homelab

  • Under the desk: one cable from the router, four wired devices next to you.
  • Next to the server shelf: the mini PC running Proxmox, the NAS and the Pi all get wired gigabit links instead of Wi-Fi.
  • Behind the TV: a console, a streaming box and a smart TV on one wall jack.

What it does not do

It is unmanaged, so there are no VLANs, no port settings and no traffic graphs. If you want to split IoT devices onto their own VLAN, you need a managed or "easy smart" switch instead (TP-Link sells those under other model numbers). If you only need more ports, unmanaged is simpler and there is nothing to misconfigure. There is also an 8-port version if five is not enough.

item.title: SanDisk 2TB Extreme Portable SSD: the pocket backup drive that replaced spinning disks
item.description: What the SanDisk Extreme Portable SSD (2TB) is, where it fits for backups and a homelab, and what it does not replace. With the short video and the Amazon link.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The Amazon link on this page supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

The short video for this product uses a fictional AI-generated presenter (AI face, voice and lip-sync). We have not personally tested this drive; the details below come from SanDisk's own product information. No price or rating is quoted because both change; check the listing.

The problem it solves

A lot of desks still back up to a spinning USB hard drive: slow, heavy, and one bad drop away from losing everything on it. A portable SSD has no moving parts, so it is faster and much harder to break in a bag.

What it is

  • Solid-state, no moving parts
  • USB-C, USB 3.2 Gen 2
  • Read speeds up to 1050 MB/s (SanDisk's figure)
  • Up to 3-meter drop protection and IP65 water and dust resistance
  • 256-bit AES hardware encryption with password protection
  • Pocket-size, with a carabiner loop to clip it to a bag
  • Also sold in 1TB and 4TB

Where it fits

  • The "1" in 3-2-1: a copy of your photos, documents or VM backups that lives somewhere other than the machine it came from.
  • Moving big files: a full laptop image or a stack of VM exports in minutes instead of an evening.
  • Travel: a backup copy that rides along without worrying about bumps.

What it does not do

One drive is not a backup strategy on its own. If it is your only copy, it is a single point of failure like any other disk. Keep at least one more copy somewhere else, and test a restore now and then. The book Never Lose Your Data walks through the whole 3-2-1 setup.

item.title: Kasa Smart Plug Ultra Mini: reboot a frozen server from the couch
item.description: What the Kasa Smart Plug Ultra Mini (EP10, 2-pack) does for a homelab: remote hard reboots, schedules, Home Assistant. And what not to put on it. With the short video and the Amazon link.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The Amazon link on this page supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

Get it on Amazon: Kasa Smart Plug Ultra Mini EP10 (2-pack)

The short video for this product uses a fictional AI-generated presenter (AI face, voice and lip-sync). We have not personally tested it; the details below come from the maker's own product information. No price or rating is quoted because both change; check the listing.

The problem it solves

Every homelab has one box that hangs: the cheap mini PC, the old router, the Raspberry Pi with the flaky SD card. When it locks up, the fix is pulling the power cord. A Wi-Fi smart plug turns that into a tap in an app, from the couch or from anywhere.

What it is

  • A Wi-Fi plug on 2.4 GHz, no hub needed
  • On and off from the Kasa app, at home or away
  • Schedules, timers and an away mode
  • Works with Alexa and Google Home
  • Home Assistant has an integration for Kasa devices
  • Ultra-mini size, so two fit in one outlet
  • Sold as a 2-pack

Where it fits

  • Remote hard reboot: put the box that freezes behind one and power-cycle it when it stops answering.
  • Schedules: desk lights, a monitor, or a test box that only needs to run in the evening.
  • Home Assistant: automate it with everything else, for example cut power to a hung device after a ping check fails (do this with care; see below).

What it does not do

A smart plug cuts power hard; it does not shut a machine down cleanly. Do not use one to switch off a NAS or a server in the middle of writes, and never put it in front of the device that runs your network or your Home Assistant, or you lose the way to turn it back on. Use it for things that are safe to yank, and keep a proper shutdown for anything with data on it. Plugs on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi also depend on your Wi-Fi being up.

item.title: Gemini Nano in your app without the guesswork: design for 'unavailable' first
item.description: Gemini Nano only runs on some phones. Here is how to check its status before every call, what each of the four states means, and the surprises that trip people up once.
item.content:encoded:
Gemini Nano is the language model that ships with the phone. But only some phones. Build the feature as if it is always there and most of your users get an error, or a button that does nothing.

This post covers how to plan for that, using Chapter 3 (Gemini Nano Without the Guesswork) of On-Device AI for Android.

How it works, in one paragraph

Gemini Nano runs inside AICore, an Android system service. AICore keeps the model updated, applies Google's safety filters and lets every app on the device share one copy. You never bundle or host the base model. You reach it through ML Kit's GenAI APIs, which come in two shapes:

  • Feature APIs for common jobs: Summarization, Proofreading, Rewriting, Image description and Speech recognition. Each one is tuned for its task and needs no prompt writing.
  • The Prompt API for everything else: your own text prompt, or an image plus text, with optional settings such as temperature and maximum output tokens.

The trap: assuming the model is there

Google's ML Kit GenAI overview page publishes the supported device list, and it differs by API. At the time of writing (October 2026) the feature APIs list recent flagships from Google (Pixel 9, 10 and 11 families), Samsung (Galaxy S25 and S26 families and recent foldables) and models from other makers. The Prompt API has its own list, grouped by Gemini Nano version. The list grows, so check it on developers.google.com/ml-kit/genai before you promise a feature.

Two more conditions from the same documentation:

  • The GenAI APIs need Android API level 26 or higher.
  • They are not supported on devices with an unlocked bootloader.

The book's advice is blunt: design for "unavailable" first. On most of your users' phones today, the Gemini Nano path will report that it cannot run. That has to lead somewhere useful.

The fix: every call starts with a status check

Each GenAI client can report one of four states. Each one has a clear next step:

StateWhat it meansWhat to do
AVAILABLEYou can run inference nowRun it
DOWNLOADABLEThe phone supports it, but the model or the feature's adapter is not on the device yetDownload, with progress
DOWNLOADINGA download is in progressWait or queue the request
UNAVAILABLEThis device cannot run it, or AICore has not fetched its latest configuration yetUse another backend

Only UNAVAILABLE sends the user elsewhere. The other three end in AVAILABLE.

The Prompt API, behind an interface

The Prompt API is version 1.0.0-beta4 at the time of writing. Its Kotlin API is coroutine-first: checkStatus() is a suspend function, download() returns a Flow, and generateContentStream() streams chunks.

dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.mlkit:genai-prompt:1.0.0-beta4")
}

The book wraps it in a TextGenerator interface, so the status maps to an availability the rest of the app understands:

class NanoGenerator : TextGenerator {
    private val model = Generation.getClient()
    override val label = "On this phone (Gemini Nano)"

    override suspend fun availability(): Availability =
        when (model.checkStatus()) {
            FeatureStatus.AVAILABLE -> Availability.Ready
            FeatureStatus.DOWNLOADABLE,
            FeatureStatus.DOWNLOADING -> Availability.NeedsDownload(null)
            else -> Availability.Unavailable("Gemini Nano is not supported here")
        }

    suspend fun downloadModel(onProgress: (Long) -> Unit) {
        model.download().collect { s ->
            if (s is DownloadStatus.DownloadProgress)
                onProgress(s.totalBytesDownloaded)
            if (s is DownloadStatus.DownloadFailed) throw s.e
        }
    }

    override fun generate(messages: List<ChatMessage>): Flow<String> {
        val prompt = messages.toPlainPrompt()     // see below
        return model.generateContentStream(prompt)
            .map { chunk -> chunk.candidates[0].text }
    }
}

The point of the interface is the fallback. When availability() says Unavailable, the app's chooser moves on to a local LiteRT-LM model or a home server, and the screen does not change.

The Prompt API takes one prompt, not a structured chat history, so toPlainPrompt() is yours to write: a short instruction line, then the last few turns as "User:" and "Assistant:" lines. Keep it well under the input limit below.

The easiest win: Summarization

If your feature is "summarize this", start with the Summarization feature API (1.0.0-beta1 at the time of writing). It needs no prompt engineering. The feature APIs return Guava ListenableFutures, so add the coroutines Guava adapter to await them:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.mlkit:genai-summarization:1.0.0-beta1")
    implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-guava:1.11.0")
}

Create the client once with the input type, the output length (one, two or three bullets) and the language. Check its status with checkFeatureStatus(), and download with downloadFeature() when it reports DOWNLOADABLE. Close the client when the screen goes away; the documentation suggests onCleared() in your ViewModel.

Input must be under 4000 tokens, roughly 3000 English words, for both Summarization and the Prompt API. For longer text, the summarization docs suggest summarizing the first 4000 tokens or turning on automatic truncation with setLongInputAutoTruncationEnabled.

Things that surprise people once

  • Fresh devices are not ready. Right after a phone is set up or AICore's data is cleared, AICore may still be initializing and fetching its configuration. The documentation advises retrying later. Treat these errors as "try again in a moment", not as "unsupported forever".
  • There is a per-app quota. AICore enforces an inference quota per app. Do not fire a request on every keystroke. Trigger generation on a deliberate action.
  • Long output is a bad fit. The docs advise against use cases that need more than 4K tokens of output.
  • It is beta. Pin the version, read the release notes on each upgrade, and keep this code behind your interface.

Checklist

  • Check the supported device list for the specific API you use.
  • Require API level 26+, and expect UNAVAILABLE on unlocked bootloaders.
  • Call the status check before every use, and handle all four states.
  • Give UNAVAILABLE a real fallback behind one interface.
  • Show download progress for DOWNLOADABLE.
  • Keep input under 4000 tokens and output use cases short.
  • Generate on a deliberate action, not per keystroke.
  • Pin the beta versions: genai-prompt 1.0.0-beta4, genai-summarization 1.0.0-beta1.

item.title: Gear the books recommend: the parts lists from Homelab the Right Way
item.description: Every piece of hardware the Homelab the Right Way books actually name, grouped by project, with the one-line reason each book gives. The Proxmox host, networking, ZFS storage, Home Assistant radios, the turtle-tank sensor build and the media server.
item.content:encoded:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. The links on this page go to Amazon; buying through them supports the blog at no extra cost to you.

This page collects the hardware the books name, in one place, with the reason each book gives for it. Where a book names an exact product, the link goes to that product. Where a book only describes the kind of thing you need (for example "a used business mini PC" or "a reptile UVB bulb"), the link is an Amazon search for that kind of thing, and the book's rule for choosing one is written next to it. Prices change every week, so there are none here; check the listing.

The Proxmox host

  • A used business mini PC (search on Amazon). Book 2 says a "tiny" or "micro" office desktop with an Intel 8th-generation or newer CPU, 16 GB of RAM and two drives "will run everything in this book with room to spare". No rack needed.
  • A small SSD, 256 to 512 GB (search on Amazon). Book 2's layout puts Proxmox and the guests' virtual disks on their own small SSD, so a dead drive never takes the server and your photos at the same moment.
  • A Raspberry Pi (search on Amazon). In a two-node cluster, Book 1 uses it as the QDevice: a tiny third vote so one node going down doesn't freeze the other. Book 12 suggests the same kind of always-on box for a second Uptime Kuma that watches your monitoring from outside.
  • A powerline or MoCA adapter (search on Amazon). Book 1's rule is that cluster nodes are wired. If a node physically can't be, one of these is "still better than Wi-Fi".
  • A UPS with a USB data port (search on Amazon). Book 12 reads it with Network UPS Tools so the Proxmox host can shut down cleanly and you get an alert when the house is on battery. Book 6 says to keep the Z-Wave stick on the same UPS, because a controller that loses power mid-write can corrupt its memory.

Networking

  • A managed switch with 802.1Q VLANs (search on Amazon). Book 5's network is built from VLANs, and every managed switch asks the same three questions per VLAN: tagged, untagged, or not a member.
  • A Wi-Fi access point that maps each SSID to a VLAN (search on Amazon). One Wi-Fi network per zone, each tagged with its VLAN, with client isolation on the guest network, which the firewall can't do for you.

Backups and storage

  • An LSI/Broadcom 9300-series HBA in IT mode (search on Amazon). Book 17 calls a used card of this class "the common homelab choice" for ZFS, because IT mode hands every disk to ZFS directly. You only need one when you run out of SATA ports or want to pass all the disks to a TrueNAS VM.
  • CMR hard drives (search on Amazon). "Use CMR drives for every ZFS pool." SMR drives can stretch a resilver from hours to days. Check the exact model number in the maker's datasheet.
  • WD Red Plus 8 TB (WD80EFPX) (on Amazon). The drive model used in Book 17's example commands (pool creation, replacing a disk, expanding a RAIDZ).
  • Samsung 990 PRO 2 TB NVMe (on Amazon). The NVMe drive in Book 17's examples. The book's two-pool design puts VM disks on fast SSDs and bulk data on hard drives.
  • A small SSD with power-loss protection (search on Amazon). Only if you actually need a ZFS SLOG (sync writes). Book 17 is clear that for SMB copies and media "a SLOG does nothing"; when you do need one, mirror it.
  • An external USB disk (search on Amazon). In Book 3's off-site options, a disk you rotate to work is best for "the thing you cannot upload". It's a fourth copy, not your only off-site one, because it depends on you remembering.

Home Assistant: Zigbee and Z-Wave

Book 6 lists the Zigbee coordinators "worth buying"; any current one works with both ZHA and Zigbee2MQTT:

  • Home Assistant Connect ZBT-1 (on Amazon) (formerly SkyConnect). Made by Nabu Casa; runs Zigbee or Thread firmware, not both at once.
  • SONOFF ZBDongle-E (on Amazon). Same chip family as the ZBT-1; "a solid budget choice".
  • SONOFF ZBDongle-P (on Amazon). Texas Instruments chip; "the long-time Zigbee2MQTT favourite".
  • SMLIGHT SLZB-06 (search on Amazon) (Ethernet/PoE). The book's reliability pick for a Proxmox homelab: the radio stays out of the rack, survives a VM migration and needs no USB passthrough.
  • A 1 to 2 m USB 2.0 extension cable (search on Amazon). If you use a USB stick, put it on one, away from the server case, SSDs and access points. USB 3.0 ports radiate noise right where Zigbee lives.
  • Mains-powered Zigbee smart plugs (search on Amazon). Only mains-powered devices route in a Zigbee mesh, so a plug in each room between the coordinator and the far sensors is "a fine use of a plug".

For Z-Wave, Book 6 says to buy an 800-series controller for your region (better range, Long Range support, SmartStart) and names these as current examples:

  • Zooz ZST39 LR (on Amazon)
  • Aeotec Z-Stick 10 (on Amazon)
  • Home Assistant Connect ZWA-2 (on Amazon)

Turtle tank: the water-sensor build

Book 4's sensor is plug-together: no soldering, no custom board. The book's parts list gives the exact listings:

  • Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32C3, pre-soldered (on Amazon). Tiny, native USB-C, Wi-Fi, and two analog pins that keep working while Wi-Fi is on. The pre-soldered version already has its headers.
  • BOJACK DS18B20 temperature sensor module kit (on Amazon). A fully submersible probe, and the kit's small adapter board has the pull-up resistor built in, so there's nothing to add.
  • KEYESTUDIO TDS Meter V1 (on Amazon). Board, probe and cable in one bag, and it runs on 3.3 V.
  • KEYESTUDIO Turbidity Sensor V1 (on Amazon). Board plus probe; set its switch to analog.
  • HiLetgo DC 0-25 V voltage sensor module (5-pack) (on Amazon). A prebuilt 5:1 divider with screw terminals. The turbidity signal goes up to about 4.5 V and the XIAO's pins take 3.3 V, so this sits between them.
  • ELEGOO 120-piece Dupont jumper wires (on Amazon). You need all three kinds (M-M, M-F, F-F), and the 120-pack has them.
  • REXQualis 400-point breadboards (6-pack) (on Amazon). Used only as a power strip, so one ground pin on the XIAO can feed every board.
  • A USB-C cable that carries data (search on Amazon). Not a charge-only cable, or the board won't flash.
  • Optional: Zulkit ABS project boxes (on Amazon) if you have no 3D printer (they fit the XIAO and a board or two), or 10 kΩ resistors (search on Amazon) to build a 2:1 divider yourself instead of the module.
  • For the printed enclosure in Chapter 8: about 100 g of ABS filament (search on Amazon).
  • The turtle cam: an ESP32-CAM (AI-Thinker, OV2640) with the ESP32-CAM-MB programmer board (search on Amazon). The bare ESP32-CAM has no USB port; the MB board snaps underneath and adds one.

Turtle tank: the habitat

Book 4 is clear that this is general guidance for aquatic turtles such as sliders. Check a care sheet for your species.

  • A reptile UVB bulb (5.0 or 10.0) (search on Amazon). The one new keepers skip. Without UVB a turtle can't make vitamin D3. Mount it with nothing between the bulb and the turtle (glass and most plastics block UVB), and replace it on a schedule, every 6 to 12 months depending on the bulb.
  • A basking heat bulb (search on Amazon). For a basking spot of about 90 to 95 °F at the surface of the dock. Keep electronics and the turbidity probe out of its beam.
  • An outlet timer (search on Amazon). Both lights on a timer, 10 to 12 hours a day.
  • A submersible aquarium heater with its own thermostat (search on Amazon). Keeps the water in the 76 to 82 °F band. A heater stuck on is the emergency the sensor's alert is for.
  • A stick-on aquarium thermometer (search on Amazon). Cheap, and "tells you whether the heater is lying". It's also the reference reading when you calibrate the probe.
  • An aquatic turtle filter (search on Amazon). Rated for two to three times your water volume: a 20-gallon tank wants a filter sold for 40 to 60 gallons. A canister filter once the tank gets big.
  • Dechlorinator (search on Amazon) for the weekly 25 to 50 percent water change.
  • A liquid test kit for ammonia, nitrite and nitrate (search on Amazon). The cheap probes are trend meters; the test kit answers "is the water safe". You want zero, zero and under about 40 ppm.
  • A 20-gallon turtle starter kit (search on Amazon). Lamp fixtures, bulbs, a thermometer and a floating dock in one box: the quickest way to get all the pieces at once. Kits usually skimp on the filter.

The media server

  • An Intel CPU with integrated graphics (search on Amazon). Book 15 does all its transcoding on Intel Quick Sync: "a single Proxmox host with an Intel CPU that has integrated graphics is enough for everything here." Avoid models ending in "F" (no integrated GPU), and check Quick Sync support on Intel's spec page before you buy.

What the books say not to buy

  • SMR drives for a ZFS pool, and RAID cards in "JBOD" or "passthrough" mode instead of an IT-mode HBA (Book 17).
  • An Intel "F" CPU for a transcoding box (Book 15).
  • A Z-Wave controller for the wrong region, or a 700-series stick on early firmware (Book 6).
  • A charge-only USB-C cable for flashing (Book 4).

item.title: Pocket Assistant: a local AI organizer for bills, notes and tasks
item.description: Pocket Assistant scans documents, organizes notes, tracks tasks and runs an AI chat on your phone, with no cloud sync and no account.
item.content:encoded:
Bills, receipts, voice memos, to-do lists and reminders tend to end up in five different apps, several of which keep a copy of your life on their servers. Pocket Assistant pulls those jobs into one organizer and keeps all of it on your phone. The AI that sorts and reads your documents runs on the device, and there is no cloud sync and no account.

What it does

Document scanning

  • Scan bills, receipts and documents.
  • The AI pulls out the key information.
  • Documents are organized by category and date.
  • Everything you scan is searchable.

Notes

  • Voice-to-text notes.
  • AI-assisted organization.
  • Tags and categories.
  • A quick-capture widget.

AI chat

  • A chat assistant for help with tasks and questions.
  • Context-aware responses.
  • Processing happens on the device.

Tasks and reminders

  • Create and manage tasks.
  • Reminders based on context.
  • Daily and weekly planning.
  • Tasks connect with your notes.

How the pieces fit together

The useful part is that these are not four separate tools. A scanned bill becomes searchable information instead of a photo in your gallery. A voice note you dictate gets organized and tagged, and it can be linked with a task. The daily and weekly planning views sit on top of the tasks and reminders, so the things you captured during the week turn into a plan.

The quick-capture widget and quick actions are there for the moment something comes up. If capturing an idea takes more than a couple of taps, it usually does not get captured at all, so a home-screen widget is worth setting up on day one.

A simple routine to start with

Based on what the app offers, a reasonable way to start:

  1. Add the widget to your home screen for quick capture.
  2. Scan the bills and receipts currently sitting on your desk.
  3. Turn your current to-do list into tasks, and attach notes where they help.
  4. Use the weekly planning view once a week to see what is coming up.

Privacy

The listing is clear on this point:

  • All data is stored on your device.
  • No cloud sync and no accounts.
  • AI processing happens on the device.
  • Your data never leaves your phone.

For an app that holds your bills and receipts, that matters. Financial documents are exactly the kind of data you might not want uploaded to an organizer's servers. The trade-off of no cloud sync is that your data lives on the one device, so it is worth knowing that before you rely on it.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download, with an optional premium upgrade mentioned in the listing.
  • Ads: the app contains ads.
  • Category: Lifestyle, rated Everyone.
  • Interface: simple design, dark mode support, a home-screen widget and quick actions.
  • No sync: everything stays on the phone it is on; there is no cloud copy.

Is it for you?

  • You have paper bills and receipts you want searchable without uploading them anywhere.
  • You capture ideas by voice and want them organized automatically.
  • You want tasks, reminders and notes in one place.
  • You prefer an organizer with no account and no cloud sync.

item.title: Snapshots on a schedule, replicas on another box: sanoid and syncoid pull replication for ZFS
item.description: ZFS snapshots undo deletions and bad upgrades, but they die with the pool. A sanoid retention policy, syncoid pull replication run from the backup box, and a monthly checksum restore turn snapshots into something you can actually recover from.
item.content:encoded:
A ZFS snapshot is a read-only picture of a dataset at one instant. It takes about a second to create and costs no space at first. Snapshots on a schedule, thinned automatically and copied to a second machine, are the single biggest upgrade most homelab storage can get. This post builds exactly that with two tools from the same project: sanoid takes and prunes snapshots, syncoid replicates them.

The trap

Homelab storage usually fails in one of two opposite ways. The first lab has no snapshots at all, so an accidental rm -rf on a share is permanent. The second takes snapshots every fifteen minutes and never prunes them: ten thousand of them, a pool that is mysteriously full, and a zfs list -t snapshot that takes a minute to answer.

Both labs also believe the snapshots are their backup. They are not. A snapshot lives in the same pool as the data. If the pool dies (two disks in a RAIDZ1, a controller that writes garbage, a mistaken zpool destroy), the snapshots die with it. Snapshots protect against changes: deletions, overwrites, bad upgrades, ransomware on a share. Backups protect against loss. You need both, and replication to a second box gets you most of the way.

Why snapshots are cheap

ZFS never overwrites data in place. When a block changes, the new version goes to a new location and the dataset's pointers move to it. A snapshot simply keeps the old pointers, so until something changes the snapshot and the live dataset share every block.

That also tells you where snapshot space goes. A snapshot grows as the live data moves away from it: delete a 20 GB folder and the space is not freed until every snapshot that still references those blocks is destroyed. When a pool fills up unexpectedly, this command sorts snapshots by the space only they hold, and the culprit is usually at the bottom:

zfs list -t snapshot -o name,used -s used

Step 1: a retention policy with sanoid

Debian and Proxmox VE package sanoid, and the package ships a systemd timer that runs it every 15 minutes:

apt install sanoid
systemctl enable --now sanoid.timer
systemctl list-timers | grep sanoid

The policy lives in /etc/sanoid/sanoid.conf: datasets at the top, templates at the bottom. A trimmed version:

[tank/documents]
	use_template = important
[tank/shares]
	use_template = standard
	recursive = yes
[tank/media]
	use_template = light

[template_important]
	frequently = 0
	hourly = 48
	daily = 30
	weekly = 8
	monthly = 12
	yearly = 0
	autosnap = yes
	autoprune = yes

[template_standard]
	hourly = 24
	daily = 14
	weekly = 4
	monthly = 3
	autosnap = yes
	autoprune = yes

[template_light]
	hourly = 0
	daily = 7
	weekly = 0
	monthly = 0
	autosnap = yes
	autoprune = yes

Each dataset section names a template, and recursive = yes applies it to every child dataset. The numbers are how many snapshots of each kind to keep. Recent history is dense (48 hourlies) and older history is sparse (12 monthlies), so about a hundred snapshots cover a full year, and sanoid deletes each one when it falls off the end of its rung.

Anything you leave out comes from /etc/sanoid/sanoid.defaults.conf, which you should not edit, so set every interval explicitly in your own templates.

Test the policy without touching anything, then take a round of snapshots and look:

sanoid --cron --readonly --verbose      # simulate
sanoid --take-snapshots --verbose       # take snapshots now
zfs list -t snapshot -o name,used -s creation tank/documents | tail -5

One rule if the box also runs Proxmox guests: pick one snapshot owner per dataset. Proxmox's own VM snapshots and storage replication create and delete snapshots on the same zvols. If Proxmox replication or vzdump with PBS already covers your guests, leave tank/vm out of sanoid, or keep its policy very light.

Step 2: how incremental replication works

zfs send turns a snapshot into a stream of bytes; zfs receive turns that stream back into a dataset on another pool. The first send is full. Every later send is incremental: only the blocks that changed between two snapshots travel. Both sides must keep the last common snapshot, or the next incremental has nothing to build on.

By hand it looks like this, with nas and backup as SSH host aliases with key-based login:

zfs snapshot tank/documents@rep-1
zfs send tank/documents@rep-1 | ssh backup zfs receive -u backup/documents
zfs snapshot tank/documents@rep-2
zfs send -i @rep-1 tank/documents@rep-2 | ssh backup zfs receive -u backup/documents

zfs receive -u does not mount the received dataset, which avoids mountpoint clashes on the target. Tracking the last common snapshot for every dataset, every night, is the part nobody keeps up with. syncoid does it for you: it finds the newest common snapshot, sends the incremental, resumes interrupted transfers when both sides support it, and cleans up its own snapshots.

Step 3: pull, do not push

A backup box that pulls from the NAS is safer than a NAS that pushes to the backup box. If the NAS is compromised, an attacker holding its SSH key can delete everything on a push target. With pull replication, the NAS has no credentials for the backup box at all.

On the backup box, a small script run by cron at 01:30:

cat > /usr/local/sbin/pull-replicas <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
S="/usr/sbin/syncoid --recursive --no-sync-snap --quiet"
$S nas:tank/photos    backup/photos
$S nas:tank/documents backup/documents
EOF
chmod +x /usr/local/sbin/pull-replicas
echo '30 1 * * * root /usr/local/sbin/pull-replicas' > /etc/cron.d/pull-replicas

By default syncoid creates its own short-lived syncoid_ snapshot for each run. --no-sync-snap tells it to use the snapshots sanoid already took, which keeps the target's history identical to the source. --recursive includes child datasets. For an encrypted dataset, add --sendoptions=w for a raw send: the blocks travel and are stored still encrypted, and the backup box never needs the key. Keep every passphrase somewhere that does not depend on the pool it unlocks.

The received datasets still need pruning. On the backup box, give them a template that never takes snapshots and only prunes what replication brings in:

[backup/photos]
	use_template = backup
	recursive = yes
[backup/documents]
	use_template = backup
	recursive = yes

[template_backup]
	autosnap = no
	autoprune = yes
	hourly = 48
	daily = 30
	weekly = 8
	monthly = 12

For tighter security, replicate as a non-root user with ZFS permission delegation: on the NAS, zfs allow -u replicator send,hold,snapshot tank, and run syncoid on the backup box with --no-privilege-elevation. The receiving user needs create,mount,receive on the target dataset. Test the delegation once by hand before relying on it.

A TrueNAS box works as the target too. It speaks standard ZFS over SSH, so the same syncoid commands work; create the destination parent dataset in the TrueNAS UI first and let TrueNAS own the retention for those datasets.

Step 4: prove it

Replication you have never restored from is a hope, not a plan. Once a month, restore one real file from the replica and compare checksums from both machines:

# On the backup box
zfs clone backup/documents@autosnap_2026-10-16_00:00:02_daily backup/restore-test
zfs set mountpoint=/mnt/restore-test backup/restore-test
sha256sum /mnt/restore-test/taxes/2025.pdf
ssh nas sha256sum /tank/documents/taxes/2025.pdf
zfs destroy backup/restore-test

Matching checksums are the proof.

Checklist

  • Every dataset that matters has a sanoid template, and tank/vm has exactly one snapshot owner.
  • sanoid.timer is enabled and zfs list -t snapshot shows recent autosnaps.
  • A second box receives incremental replication, ideally by pulling.
  • Encrypted datasets replicate raw, and the keys are stored off the pool.
  • The backup box prunes with a backup template (autosnap = no).
  • You have restored one file from the replica and compared checksums.

item.title: Your app starts slow after every update: generate a Baseline Profile and prove it is applied
item.description: After every install and update, Android runs your code interpreted and JIT-compiled until the device compiles it in the background. A Baseline Profile generated with the androidx.baselineprofile plugin makes your critical journeys fast from the first launch, and three checks prove it actually reached the device.
item.content:encoded:
A Baseline Profile is the single change most likely to make an existing Compose app start faster and scroll more smoothly without touching its logic. It is a list of the classes and methods your app needs on its most important paths, shipped inside the app, so the runtime can compile them ahead of time on install instead of discovering them slowly on the user's phone. This post generates one with the Baseline Profile Gradle plugin and then proves, three ways, that it is applied.

The trap

Your Kotlin compiles to DEX bytecode. The Android Runtime (ART) can interpret it, JIT-compile hot methods while the app runs, or run machine code compiled ahead of time (AOT). ART does not AOT-compile your whole app on install. It records which methods were used into a profile and compiles them later, when the device is idle and charging.

That works eventually, and "eventually" is the problem. After every install and every update, users start in the slow path until the device has recorded enough and found a quiet moment to compile it. Google Play's Cloud Profiles help later installs of a release, but they need time and users to build up, so they do nothing for the first users of each new version.

Jetpack libraries, Compose included, ship their own profiles, which is why a plain Compose app already benefits a little. Library profiles only cover library code, though. Your screens, ViewModels and repositories are in nobody's profile but yours. Google's documentation states that Baseline Profiles improve code execution speed by about 30% from the first launch for the code paths they include; your own gain depends on your app, and Macrobenchmark tells you what it is.

Step 1: the generator module

The Baseline Profile Gradle plugin (androidx.baselineprofile, 1.5.0) does the plumbing. Android Studio's Baseline Profile Generator module template (File > New > New Module, Android Studio Iguana or newer, AGP 8.2 or newer) writes this for you. The generator is a com.android.test module that points at the app:

// baselineprofile/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.test")
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android")
    id("androidx.baselineprofile")
}
android {
    namespace = "com.example.fieldnotes.baselineprofile"
    compileSdk = 36
    defaultConfig {
        minSdk = 28
        testInstrumentationRunner = "androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner"
    }
    targetProjectPath = ":app"
}
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.benchmark:benchmark-macro-junit4:1.5.0")
    implementation("androidx.test.uiautomator:uiautomator:2.4.0")
}

Generation needs root on the device, except on Android 13 (API 33) and newer, where Macrobenchmark can collect profiles without root. A Gradle-managed device with systemImageSource = "aosp" works everywhere because AOSP images allow root.

The app module applies the same plugin, depends on the generator, and includes ProfileInstaller:

// app/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android")
    id("androidx.baselineprofile")
}
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.profileinstaller:profileinstaller:1.4.1")
    baselineProfile(project(":baselineprofile"))
}
baselineProfile {
    saveInSrc = true      // commit the generated profile
    mergeIntoMain = true  // one profile for all variants
}

ProfileInstaller matters for installs that do not come from Google Play: sideloaded builds, internal testing installs and other stores. There, Play is not around to hand the profile to ART, so ProfileInstaller writes it on the app's first launch.

Step 2: write the journeys

The generator is an instrumented test with BaselineProfileRule. It drives the app through the paths users take every day, and the rule records every class and method that ran:

@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
@LargeTest
class BaselineProfileGenerator {
    @get:Rule val rule = BaselineProfileRule()

    @Test fun generate() = rule.collect(
        packageName = "com.example.fieldnotes",
        includeInStartupProfile = true,
    ) {
        pressHome()
        startActivityAndWait()
        device.wait(Until.hasObject(By.res("notes_list")), 5_000)

        val list = device.findObject(By.res("notes_list"))
        list.setGestureMargin(device.displayWidth / 5)
        list.fling(Direction.DOWN)
        device.waitForIdle()

        device.findObject(By.res("note_row")).click()
        device.wait(Until.hasObject(By.res("editor_body")), 5_000)
        device.pressBack()
    }
}

The test finds elements by resource id, so in Compose expose test tags as resource ids once near the root with Modifier.semantics { testTagsAsResourceId = true } and tag the elements the generator needs with Modifier.testTag("notes_list").

Good journeys follow a few rules. Cover what users actually do, most common first. Wait for content, because if the journey moves on before the list loads, the list's code is not in the profile. Keep it deterministic with local or seeded data rather than a live server. And never sign in to real accounts from a generator.

Step 3: generate and commit

Run the plugin's task, not the test directly:

./gradlew :app:generateBaselineProfile

The plugin builds the app, runs the generator and copies the result into your sources:

app/src/main/generated/baselineProfiles/baseline-prof.txt
app/src/main/generated/baselineProfiles/startup-prof.txt

Commit both. Every release build compiles them into the app, and you will find the binary form under assets/dexopt/baseline.prof in the AAB or APK. The rules inside are plain text: HSPLcom/example/fieldnotes/ui/NotesViewModel;->loadNotes()V, where H means hot, S startup and P post-startup.

The second file is a Startup Profile, produced because of includeInStartupProfile = true. It tells R8 to put every class needed at startup into the primary DEX file. It needs R8 enabled for release (isMinifyEnabled = true) and DEX layout optimization, which is on by default from AGP 8.3.

Step 4: prove it is applied

A profile that does not reach the device is just a file in a repository.

Benchmark it. Compare a fresh install with no ahead-of-time compilation against one that requires your profile and fails loudly if the app has none:

@Test fun startupNoCompilation() = startup(CompilationMode.None())

@Test fun startupBaselineProfile() = startup(
    CompilationMode.Partial(baselineProfileMode = BaselineProfileMode.Require))

Run both on the same physical device and compare the median timeToInitialDisplayMs.

Check the device by hand:

PKG=com.example.fieldnotes
adb install app-release.apk
adb shell am broadcast \
  -a androidx.profileinstaller.action.INSTALL_PROFILE \
  $PKG/androidx.profileinstaller.ProfileInstallReceiver
adb shell am force-stop $PKG
adb shell cmd package compile -f -m speed-profile $PKG
adb shell dumpsys package dexopt | grep -A 1 $PKG

The broadcast prints "1" on success, and the dexopt status should read speed-profile.

Ask from inside the app. ProfileVerifier.getCompilationStatusAsync() reports whether the profile was installed and compiled (isCompiledWithProfile, hasProfileEnqueuedForCompilation()). Log it in internal builds; "enqueued" is normal right after an install from outside Play.

Checklist

  • The generator module applies androidx.baselineprofile and targets :app.
  • The app depends on ProfileInstaller and on the generator through baselineProfile(...).
  • Journeys cover launch, the main list, opening an item, and wait for content.
  • baseline-prof.txt and startup-prof.txt are committed.
  • None versus Partial(Require) shows a measured gap on a real device.
  • dumpsys package dexopt reads speed-profile.
  • The profile is regenerated after screen redesigns, major Compose upgrades and before releases.

item.title: Ads that don't get your app flagged: AdMob's interstitial rules in plain English
item.description: AdMob's "Disallowed interstitial implementations" page in short, plus a real frequency cap from a shipping app and the two-flag check every ad call should make.
item.content:encoded:
An interstitial fires on app launch. Another fires when the user taps Back. A banner sits one finger-width from the main button. Each one looks harmless on its own. Together they produce accidental clicks, which AdMob treats as invalid traffic, and reviews that mention nothing but the ads.

This post covers what AdMob actually forbids for interstitials, how a small app turns that into a frequency cap in code, and the one check every ad call should make. It is drawn from Chapter 4 (Ad Placements That Don't Annoy) of Get Paid for Your Android App.

What AdMob forbids

AdMob's help page "Disallowed interstitial implementations" lists the patterns that get apps flagged. In short:

  • Not on app load or exit. Interstitials belong between pages of app content. For loading or returning to the app, Google recommends an app open ad instead.
  • Not after every action. The page says you should place no more than one interstitial ad after every two user actions, and that this includes tapping the Back button. No interstitial immediately after another one was closed.
  • Not in the way of navigation or the app's core content.
  • Not unexpectedly. An interstitial that appears while the user is focused on a task (playing, filling a form, reading) leads to accidental clicks. Show them only at logical breaks, and preload them so they do not pop up late, after the next screen has already appeared.

A real frequency cap

The book uses the author's TipsyBuddy app (a drink-logging app) as a worked example. Its InterstitialAdManager.kt keeps two caps and skips ads entirely for subscribers:

// From TipsyBuddy, ads/InterstitialAdManager.kt (Legacy SDK)
/** Minimum drinks logged between interstitial attempts. */
private const val MIN_ACTIONS_BETWEEN_SHOWS = 3
/** Minimum wall-clock gap between successful shows. */
private const val MIN_INTERVAL_MS = 90_000L

So an interstitial needs at least 3 logged actions and at least 90 seconds since the last one. Three actions is stricter than AdMob's two-action floor.

The file's header comment states the rule that matters most: it "fails silently if an ad cannot load" and "never blocks drink logging". An ad that is not ready is skipped, not waited for. The core action of the app always wins.

The same idea with the Next-Gen SDK

Here is the pattern written against the Next-Gen API from Google's "Load a single interstitial ad" guide. Imports from com.google.android.libraries.ads.mobile.sdk.* are omitted; Android Studio adds them.

class InterstitialController(
    private val adUnitId: String,
    private val isAdFree: () -> Boolean,
) {
    @Volatile private var ad: InterstitialAd? = null
    @Volatile private var loading = false
    private var actions = 0
    private var lastShownAt = 0L

    fun preload() {
        if (isAdFree() || ad != null || loading) return
        loading = true
        InterstitialAd.load(
            AdRequest.Builder(adUnitId).build(),
            object : AdLoadCallback<InterstitialAd> {
                override fun onAdLoaded(ad: InterstitialAd) {
                    this@InterstitialController.ad = ad; loading = false
                }
                override fun onAdFailedToLoad(adError: LoadAdError) {
                    loading = false   // try again at the next natural break
                }
            },
        )
    }

    /** Call at a natural break, e.g. after an item is saved. Main thread. */
    fun onNaturalBreak(activity: Activity) {
        if (isAdFree()) return
        actions++
        val ready = ad
        val now = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()
        val allowed = actions >= MIN_ACTIONS &&
            now - lastShownAt >= MIN_INTERVAL_MS
        if (ready == null || !allowed) { preload(); return }
        ready.adEventCallback = object : InterstitialAdEventCallback {
            override fun onAdDismissedFullScreenContent() { preload() }
            override fun onAdFailedToShowFullScreenContent(
                fullScreenContentError: FullScreenContentError
            ) { preload() }
        }
        ad = null
        actions = 0
        lastShownAt = now
        ready.show(activity)
    }

    companion object {
        const val MIN_ACTIONS = 3   // stricter than AdMob's two-action floor
        const val MIN_INTERVAL_MS = 90_000L
    }
}

What this gets right:

  1. It preloads. The ad is fetched ahead of time, so it is ready at the break instead of arriving late.
  2. It only shows at a natural break. You call onNaturalBreak() from the place in your UI where a unit of work ends, such as after an item is saved. Never on launch, never on exit.
  3. It counts actions and time. Both caps must pass.
  4. It never waits. If no ad is loaded, the moment passes and a new one is preloaded for next time.
  5. It respects paying users. isAdFree() short-circuits both loading and showing.

Call preload() once ads are ready, which in the book means after consent has been gathered and the SDK is initialized. Next-Gen also offers an ad preloading API (InterstitialAdPreloader) that keeps a cache filled for you. At the time of writing Google's guide labels it beta.

Every ad call checks the same two flags

Two rules sit above every placement decision. A user who paid to remove ads must never see one again. An app without consent must never request one. The book puts both checks in one place:

val showAds: Boolean get() = adsReady.value && !entitlements.adFree.value

adsReady covers consent and SDK setup. entitlements.adFree covers the remove-ads purchase. Every banner, interstitial and native ad reads showAds instead of making its own judgment. When one of those two facts changes, every ad in the app follows.

Checklist

  • No interstitial on app load or exit. App open ads are the format designed for cold start and returning to the app.
  • No more than one interstitial per two user actions, and Back counts as an action.
  • Never show one interstitial right after another was closed.
  • Show interstitials only at a natural break, never mid-task.
  • Preload, and skip silently when no ad is ready. Never block the core action.
  • Cap by actions and by time (TipsyBuddy uses 3 actions and 90 seconds).
  • Route every ad through one flag that checks consent and the remove-ads entitlement.

item.title: 3 numbers your turtle tank has to get right
item.description: Water at 76-82 °F, a basking spot of 90-95 °F, and a UVB bulb that is replaced on a schedule. The three numbers an aquatic turtle tank lives or dies by, why the UVB one is the one new keepers skip, and how a cheap sensor fits around them.
item.content:encoded:
A turtle tank can look perfect and still be wrong. The water is clear, the dock floats, the turtle swims around, and nothing on the outside tells you that the water is too cold to digest food or that the light over the dock has stopped doing its job months ago.

Before any electronics go near a tank, three numbers have to be right: the water temperature, the basking temperature, and UVB. No sensor fixes a tank that is set up wrong. This post walks through all three, the mistake that quietly breaks the third one, and where a water sensor actually helps.

One caveat first, straight from the book: this is general guidance for aquatic turtles such as sliders. Your species may want different numbers, so check a care sheet written for it, and ask a reptile vet if anything looks off.

Number 1: the water, 76 to 82 °F

Sliders want water in the mid to high 70s Fahrenheit, with hatchlings at the warmer end. The band the book treats as "fine" is 76 to 82 °F (about 24.5 to 28 °C).

Outside that band, things go wrong in two directions:

  • Below the low 70s, a turtle gets sluggish and stops eating.
  • Above 85 °F, he is being cooked slowly.

The tool for this is a submersible aquarium heater with its own thermostat. Add a cheap stick-on thermometer as a second opinion, because it tells you whether the heater is lying.

Gear mentioned (As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. Affiliate links.) Submersible aquarium heater with built-in thermostat · Stick-on aquarium thermometer · All the gear the books recommend

The trap: a heater that fails on

A heater that fails off is a slow problem you notice in a day. A heater that fails on is an emergency. That difference is the whole reason the water sensor in the book exists: temperature is the one reading from the build that is a real alarm.

The alert bands the book uses look like this:

Water temperatureState
76–82 °FFine
73–76 °F or 82–85 °FWarning, after two bad readings in a row
Under 73 °F or over 85 °FAlert, at once

Why bands and not a single number? A turtle does not care about 79.4 versus 80.1 °F, and a sensor that pages you every time the heater cycles is a sensor you switch off. The bands turn a wobbling line into three states, and the two-readings rule keeps one odd reading from becoming a notification.

If you run Home Assistant instead, the book describes the same alert as an ordinary automation: a numeric state trigger below 73 or above 85 °F, with a for: of 10 minutes so one odd reading does not page you, sending a notification to your phone. If the heater is on a smart plug, the same automation can turn it off above 85 °F.

Number 2: the basking spot, 90 to 95 °F

An aquatic turtle has to get fully out of the water and dry off under a warm light every day. The basking spot should be around 90 to 95 °F at the surface of the dock, with the air above the water in the low 80s. That is the heat bulb's job.

Layout matters here. Heat and light go at one end of the tank so the turtle can choose between warm-and-bright and cool-and-dim, which is how he regulates his own temperature. The heater and filter go at the other end, where the filter's current spreads the heater's warmth.

Note that the basking number is separate from the water number. It lives on the dock, not in the water, and the water sensor does not measure it.

Watch out: keep any camera and electronics box out of the basking lamp's heat and direct beam. The lamp can hit 90 °F plus at a few inches, and bright light straight into a turbidity probe makes its reading drift.

Gear mentioned (As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. Affiliate links.) Basking heat bulb / heat-and-UVB dome lamp · All the gear the books recommend

Number 3: UVB, 10 to 12 hours a day

The second bulb is UVB, and it is the one new keepers skip because the tank looks fine without it.

It is not fine. Without UVB a turtle cannot make vitamin D3, cannot use the calcium in his food, and over months his shell softens and deforms.

What the book recommends:

  • Use a reptile UVB bulb. The 5.0 and 10.0 ratings are the common ones for turtles.
  • Mount it so nothing is between the bulb and the turtle. Glass and most plastics block UVB.
  • Run both lights on a timer, 10 to 12 hours a day.
  • Write the UVB bulb's install date on it with a marker.
  • Replace it every 6 to 12 months depending on the bulb.

Gear mentioned (As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. Affiliate links.) Reptile UVB bulb · Outlet timer for the lamps · All the gear the books recommend

The trap: a bulb that still glows

UVB bulbs keep glowing long after they stop producing UVB. A bulb that looks fine can be doing nothing, which is why it gets replaced on a schedule, not when it burns out. The marker on the bulb is the schedule.

The other common mistake is mounting the UVB bulb above a glass or acrylic lid. The lid blocks most of the UVB, so the bulb is doing nothing. Mount it over an open section, at the distance the bulb's own packaging gives.

What a sensor can and cannot tell you

The book's water sensor uses three cheap probes, and it is honest about their limits:

ProbeWhat it tells you
DS18B20 (±0.5 °C)Whether the heater is doing its job; the real alarm
TDSHow much has built up since the last water change. A trend meter, not an ammonia test
TurbidityCloudiness: a clogged filter, a bacterial bloom, a messy feeding. Also a trend meter

UVB is not sensed at all; it is a note on the bulb. The basking surface is not sensed either. And a liquid test kit is still the real instrument for water safety: ammonia 0, nitrite 0, nitrate under about 40 ppm. The sensor answers "is the water warm enough, is it time for a water change, did something go cloudy". The test kit answers "is the water safe". Both together is the setup.

Gear mentioned (As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. Affiliate links.) BOJACK DS18B20 waterproof temperature sensor module kit · KEYESTUDIO TDS Meter Probe V1 sensor module · KEYESTUDIO Turbidity Sensor Module V1 · Liquid test kit for ammonia, nitrite and nitrate · All the gear the books recommend

Checklist

  • Water held at 76–82 °F by a thermostatic submersible heater, with a stick-on thermometer as a cross-check.
  • An alert for under 73 °F or over 85 °F, and warnings in the bands next to those.
  • A basking dock the turtle can fully climb out on, 90–95 °F at its surface, air above the water in the low 80s.
  • Heat and light at one end, heater and filter at the other.
  • A reptile UVB bulb (5.0 or 10.0) with nothing between it and the turtle, no glass or acrylic lid in the way.
  • Both lights on a timer, 10–12 hours a day.
  • Install date written on the UVB bulb; replaced every 6–12 months, not when it dies.
  • Electronics and probes kept out of the basking lamp's heat and beam.
  • A liquid test kit for ammonia, nitrite and nitrate, because no cheap probe replaces it.

item.title: ScamRadar: check suspicious texts, emails and links on your phone
item.description: ScamRadar uses on-device AI to judge whether a text, email, voicemail or link looks like a scam, and explains the red flags.
item.content:encoded:
A text says your package is held, a voicemail sounds like a relative in trouble, an email wants you to confirm a payment. Most people know to be suspicious; the hard part is deciding in the moment, before you click or reply. ScamRadar is built to give you a quick second opinion. You paste or share the suspicious thing, an AI model on your phone analyzes it, and you get a verdict with the reasons spelled out.

It is a second opinion, not a guarantee. A verdict helps you slow down and look at the red flags; the decision to trust a message is still yours.

What it checks

  • Text Scan. Paste a message and get one of three verdicts (Looks Safe, Suspicious, Likely Scam) with a confidence score and the red flags highlighted.
  • Email screenshots. Share a screenshot of a questionable email; text recognition runs it through the same classifier.
  • Voicemails. Import or record one, and on-device speech recognition looks for signs of AI voice cloning.
  • Links. The URL scanner opens a suspicious link in a hardened view and runs text recognition plus Safe Browsing. The Pre-Click Guard can intercept link taps and show the verdict before your browser opens.
  • Clipboard heads-up. Copy a sketchy link or a money phrase like "gift card", and a one-tap "Check this?" prompt appears.

Live Shield

Live Shield scans incoming notifications on the device from apps including Messages, WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, Gmail, Outlook, Instagram and Messenger, and shows a discreet alert when it flags a scam. It is off by default, and you choose which apps it watches.

If you already clicked or paid

This is where ScamRadar goes beyond detection:

  1. Recovery Wizard. A step-by-step checklist matched to the scam type, which you can leave and resume later.
  2. Authority reports. Pre-filled links to the right place to report it for your region, such as the FTC, IC3, BBB, Action Fraud in the UK, Scamwatch in Australia, CAFC in Canada, and 7726.
  3. Evidence (Premium). An incident report PDF and an evidence ZIP for bank disputes, police reports and insurance claims.

For family members

Care Mode is designed for someone who needs a simpler phone experience: text of 24 point or larger, a single-button flow, spoken verdicts and a "Call my family" button. With the Family plan, Trusted Contact Verification lets relatives send signed "It's really me" links to prove a message is genuine, aimed at voice-cloning impersonation, and a weekly digest summarizes the week's scans without sending message content off the devices. Anyone can share a verdict card to warn friends by SMS, WhatsApp or group chat.

Privacy

Analysis runs on the device using the Gemma 4 model, and the listing states that scanned content is never sent anywhere. No account is needed to scan. Scan history holds your last 50 scans, stays on the device, can be deleted, and is never synced. Analytics are anonymous button taps, with no message content.

Permissions are scoped: notifications for alerts, notification access only for Live Shield, the microphone only for recording voicemails, storage only when you pick a file, and internet for the optional AI model and family features. The listing says it never requests SMS, contacts, call log or accessibility permissions.

Good to know

  • Free core: text, screenshot, voicemail and URL scanning, Live Shield, the Scam Library, and Care Mode are free.
  • Premium (in-app purchase): adds the incident PDF, Evidence Locker, unlimited Shield coverage and no ads.
  • Family (subscription): extends Premium to up to 8 members, plus the weekly digest and Trusted Contact Verification.
  • Ads: the free version contains ads.
  • Not a guarantee: treat every verdict as advice, and verify through a channel you trust when money or accounts are involved.

Is it for you?

  • You get texts, emails or calls and are not always sure they are real.
  • You help an older relative stay safe on their phone.
  • You want scam checks that do not send your messages to a server.
  • You want a clear checklist if something already went wrong.

item.title: Is Jellyfin really using your GPU? A six-rung ladder to prove it on Proxmox
item.description: A transcoding setting that says QSV proves nothing. Pass an Intel iGPU into an unprivileged Proxmox container the way the Jellyfin docs recommend, then climb six checks until intel_gpu_top shows the Video engine working.
item.content:encoded:
Most of the time a media server just sends the file. Sometimes the app on the other end cannot play it: a 4K HEVC film on an old TV, a high-bitrate file on a phone on mobile data, subtitles the app cannot draw itself. Then the server converts the video while you watch. That is transcoding, and on the CPU it is slow, hot and often not fast enough for real time. An Intel integrated GPU has dedicated video engines for exactly this, and the Jellyfin documentation recommends QSV (Intel Quick Sync Video) on mainstream Intel GPUs. Getting it to work inside a Proxmox container is a short list of steps. Knowing that it works is a separate job, and the one most guides skip.

The trap: a dropdown that says QSV

Set Hardware acceleration to Intel QuickSync in the Jellyfin dashboard and the page looks done. It is not. If the container cannot open the render device, or the group number is wrong, or the source codec is not ticked for hardware decoding, Jellyfin quietly falls back to software. The film still plays. The CPU does the work. Nothing in the player tells you.

The fix is a ladder: six checks, each ruling out one failure, climbed in order. If a rung fails, fix it before climbing further.

Two things first. Intel processors whose model ends in "F" have no integrated GPU, and the Jellyfin docs say not to use them for this. And the old recipe of a privileged container with lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow lines is kept in the Jellyfin docs only for Proxmox VE 7 and older. On Proxmox VE 8 and 9 the container stays unprivileged.

Rung 1: the host has a render device

On the Proxmox host:

ls -l /dev/dri
getent group render

You should see renderD128 (and card0 or similar) owned by the render or video group. If /dev/dri is missing, the host kernel has no driver for the GPU, and nothing below will work until it does.

Gear mentioned (As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. Affiliate links.) Intel CPU with integrated graphics · All the gear the books recommend

Rung 2: the device reaches the container with the right group

Proxmox VE 8 and newer can pass a device into a container through the web interface, and the Jellyfin documentation recommends exactly this route. The detail that matters is the group id, and it is the container's group id, not the host's. Inside the container:

# inside the media container (CT 110)
getent group render
# render:x:993:      <- your number may differ

On some systems the group is video or input instead of render; use whichever exists. Then on the host, in the container's Resources tab, choose Add > Device Passthrough, enter /dev/dri/renderD128 as the device path, and set the GID in the advanced options to the number you just found. The same thing from the command line, using the dev[n] option from the Proxmox documentation:

# on the Proxmox host
pct set 110 --dev0 /dev/dri/renderD128,gid=993
pct reboot 110

After the restart, ls -l /dev/dri inside the container should show renderD128 owned by the render group. The container is still unprivileged and the host keeps using the GPU. One catch from the Jellyfin docs: you must be logged in to Proxmox as root to add device passthrough; if the option is unavailable, that is why.

If Jellyfin runs in a VM instead, the whole GPU moves into it with PCI passthrough, and the host, and every other guest, lose it.

Rung 3: Docker hands the device to Jellyfin

The official Jellyfin image already contains Intel's user-mode media drivers and the OpenCL runtime, so nothing needs installing inside it. Docker only has to pass the device through and add the group that owns it, with the number from rung 2:

# /opt/stacks/jellyfin/compose.yaml (GPU part)
services:
  jellyfin:
    image: jellyfin/jellyfin:12.2
    user: 1000:1000
    group_add:
      - "993"          # gid of render inside the LXC
    devices:
      - /dev/dri/renderD128:/dev/dri/renderD128

If you have two GPUs, the second one is usually renderD129.

Rung 4: the drivers open the GPU from inside

Before touching any Jellyfin setting, confirm the container can actually use the device. Both commands come from the Jellyfin documentation:

docker exec -it jellyfin /usr/lib/jellyfin-ffmpeg/vainfo
docker exec -it jellyfin /usr/lib/jellyfin-ffmpeg/ffmpeg -v verbose \
  -init_hw_device vaapi=va -init_hw_device opencl@va

vainfo should name the Intel iHD driver and list the supported profiles and entry points. The second command should list an Intel OpenCL device. If you get failed to initialize display or a permission error, the group in group_add does not match the group that owns /dev/dri/renderD128 inside the container. Fix the number and recreate the container.

Rung 5: the dashboard settings match your GPU

Now the transcoding settings in the Jellyfin dashboard:

  • Hardware acceleration: Intel QuickSync (QSV), or VA-API if you chose that.
  • Device: leave /dev/dri/renderD128 unless you use a second GPU.
  • Hardware decoding: tick only the codecs your GPU supports, as the docs instruct. The vainfo output and the codec tables in the Jellyfin Intel guide tell you which. Older iGPUs cannot decode HEVC 10-bit or AV1 in hardware; AV1 decoding starts with Gen 12 (11th Gen Core) graphics.
  • Enable hardware encoding.
  • Turn on tone mapping, so HDR sources look right on SDR screens. Both tone-mapping methods need a GPU with HEVC 10-bit decoding.

Rung 6: watch the GPU do the work

A setting that says "QSV" proves nothing. Make Jellyfin transcode and watch the GPU.

  1. Play a film in the web client and force a transcode by picking a lower quality in the player settings.
  2. In the dashboard, the active session should show that it is transcoding, not direct playing.
  3. On the machine that owns the GPU (the Proxmox host for a container, the VM for a VM), install and run intel_gpu_top:
apt update && apt install -y intel-gpu-tools
intel_gpu_top

The Jellyfin guide explains the engine rows: Video is the QSV decoder or encoder at work, VideoEnhance is QSV VPP processing, Render/3D covers OpenCL workloads such as tone mapping. During a hardware transcode the Video row should be busy. If every row sits at zero while the CPU climbs in top, the transcode is running in software: go back down the ladder.

When it still uses the CPU

  • Subtitles burned in. Image-based subtitles force a burn-in. It is still a video transcode, so make sure it is accelerated, and prefer text subtitles the client can render itself.
  • Codec not ticked. Jellyfin then decodes in software even when encoding on the GPU.
  • Wrong device after a reboot. With more than one GPU, render node numbers can change. Pin the right one in both the passthrough and the compose file.

Checklist

  • CPU model does not end in "F"; Quick Sync confirmed on Intel's spec page.
  • /dev/dri/renderD128 exists on the host.
  • Render group gid read inside the container; device passed with that gid; container still unprivileged.
  • Jellyfin compose file has the device under devices and the gid under group_add.
  • vainfo shows the iHD driver; the OpenCL check finds an Intel device.
  • QSV selected with only supported codecs ticked; hardware encoding and tone mapping on.
  • A forced transcode shows the Video engine busy in intel_gpu_top.
  • After a host kernel update, vainfo and a forced transcode checked again.

Once this works, most of your playback should not need it at all: direct play, where the server just sends the file, is the goal, and transcoding is the safety net underneath it.
