item.title: The permission Play rejected isn't in your manifest
item.description: Google Play reviews the merged manifest, not the one you wrote. Here is how to see what your release build really asks for, strip what a library added, and replace media permissions with the photo picker.
item.content:encoded:
Play Console flags a restricted permission on your update. You open AndroidManifest.xml, search for it, and find nothing. You never added it. It is still in the build.

That is the most common way a permission problem catches people. This post walks through why it happens and how to fix it for good, using Chapter 4 (Sensitive Permissions) of Pass Google Play Review.

The trap: you are reading the wrong manifest

Google Play treats some permissions as restricted. You may only ship them when a simpler, narrower option cannot do the job, and several need a declaration in Play Console before an update can be sent.

The surprise is rarely a permission you added. It is one a library merged in. The final manifest is a merge of yours and every dependency's. Libraries contribute permissions, services and receivers. The merged result is what ships, and it is what Play reviews. So searching your own source file and finding nothing alarming proves very little.

Step 1: look at what you actually ship

Check the permissions in the built release, not the source:

# APK: list permissions from the merged manifest
apkanalyzer manifest permissions app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk

In Android Studio you can also open your manifest and switch to the Merged Manifest tab. It shows each entry and which library contributed it. That tells you whether a permission is yours or came along with a dependency.

Step 2: remove what a library added and you don't need

tools:node="remove" takes an unwanted entry out of the merged result:

<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools">
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VIDEO"
        tools:node="remove" />
</manifest>

Run apkanalyzer on the new release build afterwards and confirm the permission is gone from the list.

Step 3: pick the narrower option first

For every restricted permission, the book's rule is to ask in a fixed order. Most features have a narrower option that needs no permission and no declaration.

PermissionNarrower option firstIf you really need it
READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEOPhoto pickerCore broad-access use only (gallery-type apps), declaration
MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGEStorage Access Framework, MediaStoreDeclaration; core need only
ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATIONForeground location while in useDeclaration form, video, prominent disclosure, privacy policy
USE_EXACT_ALARMInexact alarms, WorkManager, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARMCalendar and alarm clock apps only

Photos and videos: the picker needs no permission

Play Console Help ("Understanding Restricted Permissions with minimum scope alternatives", checked October 2026) says apps targeting Android 13 or later may only request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES and READ_MEDIA_VIDEO if system pickers like the Android Photo Picker are not sufficient for core functionality. Full compliance became mandatory on May 28, 2025.

Gallery-type apps that manage all of a user's photos qualify. An app that lets the user choose a picture to edit, attach or upload does not. A custom picker does not automatically qualify either.

The photo picker needs no permission at all. With androidx.activity 1.7.0 or higher, in Compose:

@Composable
fun AvatarPicker(onPicked: (Uri) -> Unit) {
    val pickMedia = rememberLauncherForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia()
    ) { uri ->
        if (uri != null) onPicked(uri)   // null when the user backs out
    }
    Button(onClick = {
        pickMedia.launch(
            PickVisualMediaRequest(
                ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia.ImageOnly
            )
        )
    }) { Text("Choose photo") }
}

A few details from the chapter:

  • On devices without the picker, the library falls back to ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT on its own.
  • Use PickMultipleVisualMedia(maxItems) for several items.
  • By default, access to a picked item lasts until the device restarts or the app stops. If you upload in the background, persist it:
context.contentResolver.takePersistableUriPermission(
    uri, Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION
)

The picker grants access to exactly what the user selects and nothing else. There is no permission prompt, no declaration, and nothing to justify in Play Console.

A case note from a real app

The book includes a case note from the author's own app, CaptionBurn (com.charlesh.captionburn). Play Console refused to send a CaptionBurn update with the issue "Use alternative system pickers for photos / videos". The live bundle requested READ_MEDIA_VIDEO.

The app already chose videos with PickVisualMedia, so the permission had no job. The fix removed it from the build. The current manifest in chartmann1590/captionburn strips every media and storage permission a library might merge in, with tools:node="remove":

  • READ_MEDIA_IMAGES
  • READ_MEDIA_VIDEO
  • READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED
  • READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE
  • WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE

One more detail worth knowing: the Photo and video permissions declaration page kept listing the old permission from the live bundle until the new release went live. Seeing it there after the fix does not mean the fix failed.

Checklist before you send an update

  • Read the permission list from the release build with apkanalyzer manifest permissions, not from your source manifest.
  • Check the Merged Manifest tab to see which library added each entry.
  • Remove unused library permissions with tools:node="remove".
  • Choose media with the photo picker. No READ_MEDIA_* unless the app is gallery-type.
  • Persist picked URIs with takePersistableUriPermission if you upload in the background.
  • For every other restricted permission, try the narrower option in the table first.
  • After the fix ships, expect the declaration page to show the old permission until the new release is live.

item.title: When your NFS share drops, Proxmox backups fill your root disk
item.description: If your NAS is a Directory storage on a path you mounted yourself and the mount fails at boot, vzdump writes into the empty folder on the host's root disk. Here are the three NFS backup gotchas and the fix for each.
item.content:encoded:
NFS is the most common backup target in homelabs. A NAS share is cheap, it is off the host, and Proxmox speaks it natively. It also has three classic gotchas, and the first one is nasty because nothing about it looks broken until the host itself starts failing.

The trap: the mount isn't there, but the directory is

A common way to add a NAS is to mount the share yourself, say at /mnt/backups, and then add that path to Proxmox as a plain Directory storage. It works fine, right up to the morning the mount fails at boot.

When that happens, the share is gone but the empty folder is still there. Proxmox has no way to know the folder was supposed to be a network share, so the nightly job happily writes its archives into it. That folder lives on the host's root disk.

Within a night or two, the host's root filesystem is full, and things start breaking in confusing ways. From the backup job's point of view it all looked fine: it had a target, it wrote to it, and the job finished.

This is one of the four failure modes hiding behind a reassuring green check in the Datacenter view. The storage silently isn't there, and the job either fails (good, if someone hears about it) or writes into an empty local directory and fills your root disk (very bad).

Fix 1: use the native NFS storage type

The cleanest fix is to let Proxmox own the mount. With the native NFS storage type, Proxmox manages the mount and marks the storage offline if it fails, so a dropped share becomes a failed job, not a full root disk.

pvesm add nfs nas-backup --server 192.168.10.40 --export /volume1/proxmox \
  --content backup --options vers=4.1
pvesm status

The share then appears under /mnt/pve/nas-backup, and pvesm status tells you whether Proxmox can actually reach it.

While you are there, keep the archives off the default local storage. It works, and it is the worst choice: the archives sit on the same disk as the host.

Fix 2: if you keep your own mount, mark it as a mountpoint

If you have a reason to keep a Directory storage on a path you mount yourself, tell Proxmox the path must be a mountpoint:

pvesm set nas-backup --is_mountpoint yes

That flag tells Proxmox an empty folder at that path is not enough: something has to be mounted there before it counts as the backup storage.

Gotcha 2: root squash breaks backups

vzdump writes as root. Many NAS defaults map root to nobody, which makes backups fail with permission errors.

The fix is on the NAS side: allow root access for the Proxmox hosts' IPs only. Depending on the NAS, the setting is called no_root_squash or "Map root user to admin". Scope it to the Proxmox hosts rather than opening root access to the whole network.

Gotcha 3: a hung NFS server can freeze the host's tools

A hung NFS server with a hard mount can freeze any process touching it. That includes the backup job, pvestatd and the web UI's storage view, so a NAS that stops answering can make the Proxmox host look broken too.

Two habits keep this from biting:

  • If your NAS reboots for updates at 2 a.m., schedule backups away from that window.
  • Check the storage before you trust a job.
pvesm status                    # every storage should say "active"
df -h /mnt/pve/nas-backup       # should show the NAS size, not the root disk

That df line is the quickest test for the first trap. If the size it reports is your root disk's size, the share is not mounted and anything written there is going to the host.

While you're on the share: set retention

A share that fills up causes the same pain from the other direction: nothing gets pruned, the share fills, and every job after that fails. Set retention on the storage itself, so every job that writes there inherits it:

pvesm set nas-backup \
  --prune-backups keep-last=2,keep-daily=7,keep-weekly=4,keep-monthly=3

Make sure a failure actually reaches you

The native storage type turns a dropped share into a failed job, and a failed job only helps if someone hears about it. By default, failures go to the root mailbox on the host, which nobody reads. On Proxmox VE 8.1 and later, set up a target under Datacenter → Notifications, point backup failures at it, and then force a failure on purpose to prove it works:

vzdump 101 --storage does-not-exist

If no message arrives, fix that before anything else.

Checklist: NFS backup storage

  • Backup storage is native NFS (or PBS), or has is_mountpoint set
  • Archives are not on the default local storage
  • The NAS allows root only for the Proxmox hosts' IPs (no_root_squash / "Map root user to admin")
  • Backups are scheduled away from the NAS's update and reboot window
  • pvesm status shows every storage as "active"
  • df -h /mnt/pve/nas-backup shows the NAS size, not the root disk
  • Retention is set on the storage with --prune-backups
  • A forced failure produces a notification you actually read

item.title: Ten quick edits should not queue ten syncs: unique work in WorkManager, done right
item.description: Enqueue a sync every time a note is saved and a burst of edits queues a burst of uploads. WorkManager's unique work, the right ExistingWorkPolicy, and retry classification that returns retry() only for transient errors keep an offline-first app from syncing against itself.
item.content:encoded:
The user saves a note on the subway and puts the phone in their pocket. Android may kill your process a minute later. The note still has to reach the server when the train comes up for air, maybe in an hour, maybe tomorrow. That is persistent work, and on Android persistent work means WorkManager. Google's offline-first guide says as much: draining an offline queue is persistent work that is often delegated to WorkManager.

WorkManager 2.12.0 is the stable release at the time of writing (October 2026). It stores every request in its own database, so scheduled work survives process death and reboots. The scheduling part is easy. The part that goes wrong is how many syncs you schedule, and what the worker says when one fails.

The trap: one sync per save

The obvious design is to enqueue a SyncWorker from the repository every time a row is written. It works in the emulator. Then a user edits a note ten times in a minute, and ten syncs are queued. Each one pushes the same dirty rows, each one pulls the same pages, and two of them can run at the same time against the same database. Add a retry on a flaky connection and the queue grows faster than it drains.

The fix is three decisions, all of them one line each: make the push unique work, pick the right policy for duplicates, and return Result.retry() only for errors that can actually clear up on their own.

Fix 1: unique work with the right policy

enqueueUniqueWork (one-time) and enqueueUniquePeriodicWork (periodic) take a name and a policy for what to do when unfinished work with that name already exists. For one-time work, ExistingWorkPolicy has four options:

  • REPLACE cancels the existing work and enqueues the new request.
  • KEEP ignores the new request and keeps the existing one.
  • APPEND adds the new work to the end of the existing chain.
  • APPEND_OR_REPLACE appends unless the existing chain has failed or been cancelled, in which case it starts fresh.

For a push, KEEP is the right one. If a sync is already queued, it will pick up every dirty row when it runs, including the one just saved, so the new request adds nothing.

object SyncScheduler {
    private const val PUSH = "notes-push"
    private const val PERIODIC = "notes-periodic"

    fun requestPush(context: Context, wifiOnly: Boolean) {
        val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
            .setConstraints(syncConstraints(wifiOnly))
            .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .build()
        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .enqueueUniqueWork(PUSH, ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, request)
    }

    fun schedulePeriodic(context: Context, wifiOnly: Boolean) {
        val request = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(6, TimeUnit.HOURS)
            .setConstraints(syncConstraints(wifiOnly))
            .build()
        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .enqueueUniquePeriodicWork(PERIODIC, ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, request)
    }
}

Call schedulePeriodic from Application.onCreate(); with KEEP it is harmless to call on every launch. Periodic work has a floor: the minimum repeat interval is 15 minutes, the same as JobScheduler. A flex interval lets it run within a window at the end of each period rather than at an exact moment.

Fix 2: constraints that match the user's settings

Constraints make WorkManager wait for the right conditions. For sync, a connected network is usually enough, plus the user's Wi-Fi-only setting:

fun syncConstraints(wifiOnly: Boolean) = Constraints.Builder()
    .setRequiredNetworkType(if (wifiOnly) NetworkType.UNMETERED else NetworkType.CONNECTED)
    .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
    .build()

One consequence is easy to miss: if a constraint stops being met while the worker runs, WorkManager stops the worker and retries it later. Your doWork must be safe to stop at any suspension point, which is one more reason every sync step should be idempotent.

Fix 3: retry only what can succeed later

When a worker returns Result.retry(), WorkManager waits for the backoff delay and runs it again. Result.failure() stops it, and fails everything chained after it. Deciding which errors are transient (timeouts, HTTP 5xx, 429) and which are permanent (401 after a token refresh, 400 for a malformed payload) is the most important line of sync code you will write:

class SyncWorker(
    context: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters,
    private val sync: SyncEngine,
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = when (sync.syncOnce()) {
        SyncOutcome.Done -> Result.success()
        SyncOutcome.Transient -> if (runAttemptCount < 5) Result.retry() else Result.failure()
        SyncOutcome.Permanent -> Result.failure()
    }
}

The backoff numbers come from the WorkManager guide: the delay can be no less than 10 seconds, the policy is LINEAR or EXPONENTIAL, and the default is EXPONENTIAL with a 30-second delay. That is the exponential backoff the offline-first guide recommends for network reads and queued writes, for free: your code only classifies the failure and returns retry(), with no sleep loop of its own. Cap attempts with runAttemptCount, as above, so a permanently broken request does not retry forever.

A worker with constructor parameters beyond context and params needs a WorkerFactory. With Hilt, annotate it with @HiltWorker and use HiltWorkerFactory; without DI, register a custom factory through Configuration.Provider in your Application and disable the default initializer in the manifest.

Chains, expedited work and the foreground rules

Work can run in sequence, each step's output becoming the next step's input. A chain is the natural shape for "upload attachments, then push notes, then pull":

WorkManager.getInstance(context)
    .beginUniqueWork("full-sync", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, uploadAttachments)
    .then(pushNotes)
    .then(pullNotes)
    .enqueue()

The chaining guide's failure rule: when a step fails or is cancelled, every dependent step is marked failed or cancelled too. Keep chains short and make each step meaningful on its own, so a failure tells you something.

When the user is waiting (they tapped "Sync now"), mark the request expedited with setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST), so an exhausted quota degrades to normal work instead of dropping it. On Android versions before 12, WorkManager may run expedited work as a foreground service, so any worker used with setExpedited must implement getForegroundInfo(); leaving it out can crash on older platform versions.

For a long first sync, a CoroutineWorker can call setForeground() to run as a foreground service with an ongoing notification. If your app targets Android 14 (API 34) or higher, you must specify a foreground service type for every long-running worker, declare it in the manifest by merging it into WorkManager's own service, and request the matching permission (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC for sync). Starting with Android 16, the guide notes, long-running workers can exhaust your app's job quota. For most apps the honest design is a sync that does a bounded amount of work per run and lets the next run continue, rather than one heroic foreground session.

Show the state from the repository, not the worker

To display "Syncing..." or "Last sync failed", observe the unique work's state as a Flow with getWorkInfosForUniqueWorkFlow("notes-push") and map RUNNING, ENQUEUED and FAILED to UI states. The worker itself never touches the UI.

Checklist

  • The push is unique work named once, enqueued with ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP.
  • Periodic sync is unique too, scheduled from Application.onCreate(), interval 15 minutes or more.
  • Constraints read the user's Wi-Fi-only setting; doWork is safe to stop at any suspension point.
  • retry() only for timeouts, 5xx and 429; failure() for 400 and 401 after a refresh.
  • Attempts capped with runAttemptCount; backoff left to WorkManager.
  • Chains short; a failed step fails its dependents, and that is intended.
  • Expedited workers implement getForegroundInfo(); long-running workers declare a foreground service type when targeting API 34+.
  • Every sync step is idempotent, because a stopped worker runs it again.

A sync that outlives the app is not the clever part. The clever part is making sure only one of them runs, and that it gives up at the right moment.

item.title: LiveCaptionN: live captions and translation over any Android app
item.description: LiveCaptionN floats real-time captions and translation over any app, offline on your phone or through your own Whisper server.
item.content:encoded:
Captions help in more situations than people expect. A video in another language, a noisy room, a call where the audio keeps dropping, a lecture you want to review later, or simply hearing difficulties. LiveCaptionN puts real-time captions in a floating window over whatever app you are using, and it can translate them as they appear.

What makes it interesting for a homelab audience is that it gives you two ways to process speech: fully on the phone, or on a server you run yourself.

What it does

  • Floating overlay. A resizable, draggable caption window sits over any app. You can pause, minimize or restyle it.
  • Two audio sources. Capture from the microphone, or capture internal system audio directly on Android 10 and later.
  • Streaming transcription. Low-latency speech-to-text from the streaming Vosk engine.
  • Live translation into 59+ languages using Google ML Kit or a self-hosted LibreTranslate instance.
  • Transcript history. Search, review and export timestamped caption logs.
  • Customization. Font size, text color, background opacity and position.
  • Localized interface in 59 languages.

Two processing modes

On-device

Everything runs on the phone, without internet access. You download a Vosk speech model and the ML Kit language packs you want, and after that your audio and captions never leave the device. There is no account sign-up and no tracking.

Self-hosted

You run OpenAI Whisper ASR and LibreTranslate on your own computer or home server, which the listing describes as Docker-ready. You start the container on the PC or server, then enter its local network address in the app settings. The listing's example is a LAN address such as 192.168.1.50 on port 9000.

The trade is clear. The heavy processing moves from the phone to your machine, which saves battery and CPU on the phone and gives you Whisper's accuracy. The app includes an interactive tutorial for this mode with video and audio guidance.

Hardware check

The app checks your hardware at startup and recommends a mode.

ModeMinimumRecommended
On-device2.5 GB RAM, 4 CPU cores, 350 MB free storage4 GB+ RAM, 64-bit multi-core CPU, 1.5 GB free for large models
Self-hosted1.5 GB RAM, Android 9.0 (API 28), on your home Wi-Fi or LAN

Devices under 2.5 GB of RAM or 4 cores are routed to self-hosted mode automatically, and devices with 2.5 to 3.8 GB get performance recommendations and lighter models. Self-hosted mode is how an older or budget phone can still get good captions.

Privacy and permissions

The listing states that audio streams and transcripts never leave your device or your local network. The permissions it asks for:

  • Microphone, to capture live speech.
  • Display over other apps, for the floating captions.
  • Foreground service, to keep captions running while you multitask.

item.title: Self-host your photos, files and passwords the safe way
item.description: Immich, Nextcloud and Vaultwarden on one small box at home, without the six classic traps: one disk for everything, a database on a network share, open signups, forwarded ports, a backup that isn't one, and updates that are never or always.
item.content:encoded:
Your photos, your files and your passwords, running on a small box in your house. That is the whole promise of self-hosting your life: Immich instead of Google Photos, Nextcloud (or Syncthing) instead of Drive, Vaultwarden instead of a cloud password manager.

None of the individual installs is hard. What goes wrong is the layout around them. Each stage of the build has one classic trap, and each trap has a short, documented fix. Here is the path end to end.

Trap 1: one disk, one bad day

The most common beginner layout is a single SSD holding Proxmox, the containers and every photo you own. When that SSD wears out or fills up, you lose the server and the data at the same moment, and the restore needs the very disk that died.

The fix: separate the system from the data. A small SSD (256 to 512 GB) holds Proxmox and the guests' virtual disks, databases included. A second, large drive holds the photo library, the Nextcloud files and backups waiting to go elsewhere.

Then run all three apps in one Debian 13 VM as a Docker host. Immich's documentation recommends a full VM and calls Docker inside an LXC container not recommended, possible only for advanced users. Give the VM at least 8 GB of RAM (12 to 16 GB is comfortable) and set its CPU type to host or x86-64-v2-AES, because Immich's machine-learning container needs the x86-64-v2 instruction level.

Inside the VM, mount the data disk by its label, with nofail:

mkfs.ext4 -L data /dev/sdb
mkdir -p /srv/data
echo "LABEL=data /srv/data ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2" >> /etc/fstab
mount -a && df -h /srv/data

The label means a reordered disk never mounts in the wrong place, and nofail means a missing disk still lets the VM boot so you can fix it over SSH.

Gear mentioned (As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. Affiliate links.) Used business mini PC · Small SSD, 256-512 GB, for Proxmox and guest disks · All the gear the books recommend

Trap 2: the Immich database on a network share

Immich keeps your files on disk and everything else (who is in the photo, which album it belongs to, where the file lives) in Postgres. The documentation is blunt: the database belongs on local SSD storage, never on a network share of any kind. Point DB_DATA_LOCATION at the NAS and a network hiccup during a write can leave Postgres corrupted and the timeline empty.

The second Immich trap is the version: the server only talks to mobile apps of a compatible major version, so running latest with auto-updates can silently stop your phone backups.

The fix is a handful of lines in .env:

UPLOAD_LOCATION=/srv/data/immich
DB_DATA_LOCATION=/opt/immich/postgres
IMMICH_VERSION=v3
DB_PASSWORD=ChangeMeToALongRandomString

Library on the data disk, database on the SSD, pinned to the major version. Use only letters and digits in the password; the docs warn that special characters confuse Docker's parsing. Turn on the storage template (Administration → Settings → Storage Template) before the first upload, so the library on disk is a readable year/month/day tree.

Trap 3: the hand-built Nextcloud

Web server, PHP, database, Redis, cron jobs and a dozen tuning settings, all by hand. Each piece is easy; together they are a full-time hobby, and months later the admin page is a wall of warnings.

The fix: first decide honestly what you need. A folder that stays the same on your laptop and phone is a Syncthing job. Documents, family sharing, calendars and contacts is a Nextcloud job, and then Nextcloud All-in-One (AIO) is the way: the official Docker setup that runs and updates the whole stack for you. Set NEXTCLOUD_DATADIR=/srv/data/nextcloud in the start command before the first start, because it can't be changed later without a fiddly migration. And don't rename the nextcloud-aio-mastercontainer container; AIO's self-updates depend on that exact name.

Trap 4: open signups and plain HTTP on Vaultwarden

Leave registration open and anyone who finds your URL can create an account; bots scan for exactly that. Serve it over plain HTTP and the web vault fails, because it relies on browser crypto APIs that most browsers only allow over HTTPS.

The fix is in the compose file:

SIGNUPS_ALLOWED: "false"
INVITATIONS_ALLOWED: "true"
SHOW_PASSWORD_HINT: "false"
ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:8081:80"

Generate the admin token as an Argon2 hash with docker run --rm -it vaultwarden/server /vaultwarden hash, paste it in, and double every one of its five dollar signs, or Docker Compose silently breaks it. Then chmod 600 /opt/vaultwarden/compose.yaml, turn on two-step login, and print an emergency sheet with your vault URL, email and master passphrase.

Trap 5: forwarding ports to everything

Forward port 443 on the router to the server and every service is reachable from the whole internet; within hours your logs fill with bots trying /admin and /wp-login.php.

The fix: Tailscale on the Docker VM as a subnet router, so your phone reaches home with no open router ports:

tailscale up --advertise-routes=192.168.10.0/24

Approve the route in the admin console and disable key expiry for the server. For real HTTPS names, use a reverse proxy with a wildcard certificate from the DNS challenge, with *.example.com pointing at the proxy's private address. If family members need a shared album link, forward only 443, only to the proxy, and never expose Vaultwarden or the AIO admin interface.

Trap 6: the backup that isn't one, and updates that are never or always

A file copy of a running database can restore as garbage. For Vaultwarden, use its built-in online backup in a nightly script:

docker exec vaultwarden /vaultwarden backup
tar -czf /srv/data/backups/vw-$(date +%F).tgz \
  -C /opt/vaultwarden data compose.yaml

Put the whole Docker VM on Proxmox Backup Server with a nightly snapshot-mode job, add an off-site copy, and test a restore once a quarter. On the bad day, restore passwords first: Vaultwarden comes back from the newest vw-*.tgz on any Linux machine with Docker, and it unlocks everything else.

For updates, never updating leaves known holes open, and auto-pulling every new image lands breaking releases at 3 AM. Pick a monthly maintenance hour and snapshot before touching anything:

qm snapshot 201 pre-update-$(date +%Y%m%d)
cd /opt/immich
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d

On the Proxmox host itself, use apt full-upgrade, never plain apt upgrade. Then test each app, and delete the snapshot so it doesn't slowly fill thin storage.

Checklist

  • System and guest disks on an SSD; photos and files on a separate data drive mounted by label with nofail
  • One Debian 13 VM as the Docker host, CPU type host or x86-64-v2-AES
  • Immich: DB_DATA_LOCATION on local SSD, IMMICH_VERSION=v3, storage template on before the first upload
  • Nextcloud via AIO with NEXTCLOUD_DATADIR set before the first start, or Syncthing with file versioning on
  • Vaultwarden: signups off, HTTPS only, Argon2 admin token with doubled dollar signs, two-step login, emergency sheet printed
  • Tailscale subnet router, key expiry off; no ports forwarded except 443 to the proxy if you must share
  • Nightly PBS job, Vaultwarden online backup in cron, an off-site copy, a dated quarterly restore test
  • A monthly update hour that starts with a snapshot

item.title: Pawdub: your dog finally has subtitles (and yes, it's a joke app that really listens)
item.description: Pawdub puts funny movie subtitles on your dog or cat when it actually barks or meows. Real on-device sound and scene detection, 8 personas, 59 languages, no account and nothing uploaded. It is a joke app and says so. Coming soon to Google Play.
item.content:encoded:
Your dog barks at the front door. A subtitle fades in under him: "THE MAILMAN HAS RETURNED. I WILL HANDLE THIS." That is the whole idea behind Pawdub, a new Android app from Hartmann Studios. It is for fun, and it says so on the first screen: no app can translate animals, and Pawdub never claims to. What it does do is listen and look for real, then pick a line that fits.

What actually happens

Point the camera at your dog or cat. The app listens for a bark, whine, growl, howl, meow, purr or hiss, detected on your phone. When it hears one, a movie-style subtitle appears. No sound, no subtitle. It also looks at the scene (a door, a food bowl, the couch, a toy, a bed), so the joke matches the moment: a cat at the window gets a different line than a cat at an empty bowl.

The lines themselves are jokes written for each persona. They are not a reading of what your pet means, and the app gives no advice about your pet's health, mood, training or behaviour. If you are worried about your pet, talk to a vet.

Personas

Eight of them: Drama Queen, Golden Retriever Energy, Grumpy Old Man, Royal Highness, Tiny Gremlin, Food Critic, Conspiracy Theorist and Noir Detective. Each one has its own voice and its own set of lines, so the same bark becomes a very different movie depending on who is "talking".

59 languages, offline

Subtitles come in English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic and 50 more. Each language is downloaded from Google once and then works offline. Pro adds bilingual subtitles.

Clips you already have

Open a video from your gallery and Pawdub adds subtitles to the moments where your pet makes a sound. Styles: Cinema and Meme are free; Pro adds Bubble (a speech bubble that follows your pet) and Text message.

The rest

  • Pet voices: hear the line read aloud with your phone's text-to-speech.
  • Pet profiles for every dog and cat in the house.
  • Bark diary: a log of what your pet "said" today.
  • Stickers and poster templates made from your clips.
  • Export to your gallery and share anywhere.

Free and Pro

Free: unlimited live dubbing, a few exports a day with a small Pawdub tag, 3 personas, your language plus one more, the Cinema and Meme styles, and a starter sticker pack. Ads appear in the free version, never on the camera screen.

Pro: every persona, all languages, every style, all voices, longer gallery clips, write your own lines, unlimited exports without the tag, and no ads. It is sold as a subscription with a free trial for new subscribers, or as a one-time lifetime unlock; prices are shown in Google Play.

Privacy

Everything runs on your phone with on-device AI. The microphone and camera are used only while the camera screen is open, audio and video are processed on the device and never uploaded, and there is no account. Delete a clip from the library, or everything from Settings > Delete all data. The privacy policy is at chartmann1590.github.io/pawdub-site/privacy.

Pawdub has been submitted to Google Play and is in review. Until the listing is live, the Pawdub site has the screenshots and the promo video; this post gets the Play link the day it goes live.

item.title: Upgrading to AGP 9: the Kotlin plugin you can delete
item.description: Since Android Gradle plugin 9.0, Kotlin is built into AGP. Here is what to remove, what to move, why kapt has to go, and the one icons dependency Material 3 stopped adding for you.
item.content:encoded:
You open an older Android project, bump the Android Gradle plugin to 9, and sync. The build stops with one of two messages: "Cannot add extension with name 'kotlin'" or "The 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.android' plugin is no longer required". Nothing in your code changed. The build files did not keep up with AGP.

This post covers what changed in AGP 9, the small set of edits that fix it, and two related surprises: kapt and the Material icons. Everything here comes from Chapter 2 (Thinking in Composables) and Chapter 8 (Saving Data: Room and DataStore) of Compose Without the Confusion.

The trap: applying Kotlin twice

Since Android Gradle plugin 9.0, Kotlin support is built into AGP itself. You no longer apply the separate org.jetbrains.kotlin.android plugin. Older projects apply it anyway, because that was the rule for years. With AGP 9 the plugin and AGP both try to set up Kotlin, and the sync fails with the messages above.

There is a second leftover in most older modules: an android { kotlinOptions { } } block. That block belonged to the old plugin, so it has to move too.

The fix: three edits

Google documents the migration for built-in Kotlin. In short:

  1. Remove the kotlin-android plugin from your build files.
  2. Remove it from your version catalog as well, so nothing re-adds it.
  3. Move any android { kotlinOptions { } } block to kotlin { compilerOptions { } }.

One plugin stays. You still apply the Compose compiler plugin. It ships with Kotlin and uses the same version number, so it points at the kotlin version in your catalog.

What a working AGP 9 setup looks like

Here is the version catalog from the book's sample project, using the versions current at the time of writing (October 2026):

# gradle/libs.versions.toml (excerpt)
[versions]
agp = "9.4.0"
kotlin = "2.4.21"
ksp = "2.3.12"
composeBom = "2026.09.00"
activity = "1.13.0"
lifecycle = "2.11.0"

[libraries]
compose-bom = { module = "androidx.compose:compose-bom", version.ref = "composeBom" }
compose-ui = { module = "androidx.compose.ui:ui" }
compose-ui-tooling = { module = "androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling" }
compose-ui-tooling-preview = { module = "androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling-preview" }
compose-material3 = { module = "androidx.compose.material3:material3" }
compose-icons-core = { module = "androidx.compose.material:material-icons-core" }

[libraries.activity-compose]
module = "androidx.activity:activity-compose"
version.ref = "activity"

[plugins]
android-application = { id = "com.android.application", version.ref = "agp" }
kotlin-compose = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose", version.ref = "kotlin" }

Notice what is missing from [plugins]: there is no kotlin-android entry. The only Kotlin-related plugin is kotlin-compose, and its version is the Kotlin version.

The module build file is just as short:

// app/build.gradle.kts (excerpt)
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.android.application)
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose)
}

android {
    namespace = "com.example.pantry"
    compileSdk = 36   // use the newest stable API level your AGP supports
    defaultConfig {
        applicationId = "com.example.pantry"
        minSdk = 24
        targetSdk = 36
        versionCode = 1
        versionName = "1.0"
    }
    buildFeatures { compose = true }
}

Two plugins. No kotlinOptions inside android { }. If your module still has compiler flags, they go in a top-level kotlin { compilerOptions { } } block instead.

The second trap: kapt

If your project uses Room, Hilt or another annotation processor through kapt, the plugin cleanup is not the end. With AGP 9's built-in Kotlin, the old kotlin-kapt plugin is not compatible. Google's migration guide recommends moving to KSP, and offers com.android.legacy-kapt only as a stopgap. Room, Hilt and most annotation processors support KSP today.

Moving Room to KSP is a few lines. The catalog gets the KSP and Room plugins (the ksp version is already in [versions] above):

# gradle/libs.versions.toml (additions)
[versions]
room = "2.8.5"

[libraries]
room-runtime = { module = "androidx.room:room-runtime", version.ref = "room" }
room-ktx = { module = "androidx.room:room-ktx", version.ref = "room" }
room-compiler = { module = "androidx.room:room-compiler", version.ref = "room" }

[plugins]
ksp = { id = "com.google.devtools.ksp", version.ref = "ksp" }
room = { id = "androidx.room", version.ref = "room" }

And the module applies them, swapping kapt(...) for ksp(...) on the compiler:

// app/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    // ...
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp)
    alias(libs.plugins.room)
}

room {
    schemaDirectory("$projectDir/schemas")
}

dependencies {
    implementation(libs.room.runtime)
    implementation(libs.room.ktx)
    ksp(libs.room.compiler)
}

The Room Gradle plugin's schemaDirectory writes a JSON description of every database version into your project. Commit those files. Room uses them for automatic migrations and for migration tests.

Hilt works the same way. It is built on Dagger and processed with KSP. At the time of writing the Dagger and Hilt release is 2.60.1.

The third trap: icons that stop resolving

This one is not AGP, but it tends to arrive in the same upgrade. Since Material 3 1.4.0, the library no longer pulls in material-icons-core for you. Its release notes say so. After the upgrade, Icons.Default.Add suddenly does not resolve, and the error looks unrelated to anything you touched.

The fix is to add the artifact yourself. It is already in the catalog above as compose-icons-core, and the BOM still manages its version:

dependencies {
    implementation(platform(libs.compose.bom))
    implementation(libs.compose.ui)
    implementation(libs.compose.material3)
    implementation(libs.compose.icons.core)   // Icons.Default.*
    implementation(libs.compose.ui.tooling.preview)
    implementation(libs.activity.compose)
    debugImplementation(libs.compose.ui.tooling)
}

The BOM line is the one that saves you the most pain. You declare one BOM version and leave the version off every individual Compose library. The BOM picks a set of versions that were tested together.

Checklist for an AGP 9 upgrade

  • Remove org.jetbrains.kotlin.android from every module and from the version catalog.
  • Move android { kotlinOptions { } } to kotlin { compilerOptions { } }.
  • Keep the Compose compiler plugin (org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose) at your Kotlin version.
  • Replace kapt with KSP. Use com.android.legacy-kapt only as a stopgap.
  • For Room, add the Room Gradle plugin, set schemaDirectory, and commit the schema files.
  • If Icons.Default stops resolving, add material-icons-core and let the BOM version it.
  • Leave versions off individual Compose libraries and let one BOM version pick them.

Go deeper: Compose Without the Confusion

item.title: MeshTalk: chat and talk over Bluetooth mesh with no signal
item.description: MeshTalk connects nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh for text, group chat and walkie-talkie voice. No internet, no accounts, no servers.
item.content:encoded:
Every messaging app you use depends on the same thing: a working connection to the internet. On a trail, at a crowded festival, or after a storm knocks out service, that dependency is exactly what fails. MeshTalk works without it. It uses Bluetooth mesh networking to connect phones directly to each other, with no internet, no cellular service, and no router or hotspot.

How the mesh works

In a mesh, each phone is both a client and a relay. MeshTalk connects to nearby devices automatically, and messages hop from device to device to reach their destination. The listing's point is that this works in areas with no signal at all, because nothing in the chain needs a tower or a server.

The practical consequence is that the more people nearby are running the app, the more paths a message has to travel.

What it does

Text chat

  • Send messages to anyone in range.
  • Group chats.
  • Message history.
  • Read receipts.

Voice

  • Walkie-talkie style voice.
  • Full-duplex audio, so both sides can talk at once.
  • Multiple channels.
  • Low battery use, according to the listing.

On-device AI

  • AI message suggestions.
  • Smart reply generation.
  • Translation between languages.
  • All AI features run locally on the phone.

The translation feature is a useful addition for an app like this. If you are at an event or travelling with people who speak another language, the translation still works when nobody has signal, because it does not depend on a server.

Privacy

MeshTalk has no accounts and no phone numbers. Messages stay on the devices, there is no cloud and there are no servers, and the listing describes it as end-to-end by design. Since there is no central server in the system, there is no central copy of your conversations to leak.

Where it makes sense

The listing names four situations:

  1. Hiking, camping and outdoor events, where coverage is weak or nonexistent.
  2. Disaster preparedness, for when normal networks are down.
  3. Crowds with poor signal, where the cell network is overloaded even though it technically exists.
  4. Privacy-conscious users, who want a messenger with no account and no server.

For the preparedness case, the thing to remember is that you set this up before you need it. Install the app on the phones of the people you would want to reach, and try it once while everything is working.

Good to know

  • Price: free to download, with an optional premium upgrade mentioned in the listing; the Play listing also notes in-app purchases.
  • Ads: the app contains ads.
  • Range: messages reach people in range, extended by hops between other devices running the app.
  • Everyone needs it: the mesh only includes phones running MeshTalk, so the people you want to talk to need it installed too.
  • No sign-up: no account and no phone number are needed.

Is it for you?

  • You hike, camp or go to events where your phone usually shows no bars.
  • You want a way to reach family or a group if networks go down.
  • You want walkie-talkie style voice between phones without extra hardware.
  • You want a messenger with no account, no phone number and no server.

item.title: The two decisions you can't undo before your first Google Play upload
item.description: Your application ID and your signing setup are the two Android decisions that are expensive to change after the first upload. Here is how to get both right, plus the versionCode rule that catches people later.
item.content:encoded:
Most of an Android project can be changed later. A screen can be redesigned, a library swapped, a name on the store edited. Two things are different. The application ID and the signing setup are decided before your first upload, and changing either one afterwards ranges from painful to impossible.

Both take minutes to get right. Here is what to do, with the code from Ship Your First Android App.

The trap: com.example goes live

Every tutorial starts with com.example.something. It works fine on your phone, so it is easy to forget. Then the first bundle goes up to Play Console and the placeholder becomes the app's permanent identity.

Android's documentation is blunt about this. Once you publish, you should never change the applicationId in app/build.gradle.kts, because if you change it, Google Play treats the upload as a completely different app. Your installs, ratings and reviews stay with the old ID.

The fix: pick an ID you can live with forever

The naming rules from developer.android.com:

  • At least two segments, separated by dots.
  • Each segment starts with a letter.
  • Only letters, digits and underscores: [a-zA-Z0-9_].

The convention is your domain, reversed, plus the app: com.yourname.torchlight. If you have no domain, a reversed form of a name you control works. What matters is that it is unique and yours. Replace com.example before the first upload, while it is still free to change.

One thing that confuses people: namespace and applicationId start out identical, but they are different things. The namespace is only the Kotlin package for the generated R and BuildConfig classes and can be refactored any time. The application ID is the public identity. Changing one does not change the other.

The second decision: how your app is signed

Every Android app is signed, and devices only install an update signed by the same key as the installed version. Google Play splits this into two keys:

KeyWho holds itWhat it signsIf you lose it
Upload keyYou, in a keystore file (.jks)The bundle you upload to Play ConsoleGoogle can reset it; you request a reset
App signing keyGoogle PlayThe APKs delivered to users' devicesNothing to lose; Google keeps it

Play App Signing is required for new apps, and new apps are automatically enrolled with Google-generated keys. Your job is only the upload key. Play Console asks for an RSA key of 2048 bits or more in a Java keystore, and Android's signing guide recommends a validity of at least 25 years:

keytool -genkeypair -v \
  -keystore upload-keystore.jks \
  -alias upload \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 \
  -validity 10000

-validity is in days. 10,000 days is a little over 27 years.

Where the key must not live

The common mistake is keeping the keystore in the project folder and committing it to Git, or keeping the only copy on one laptop. Store the .jks file outside the repository, back it up in at least two places (for example an encrypted cloud drive and a USB stick), and keep the passwords in a password manager. Google can reset a lost upload key, but a reset takes a support request and waiting, and a leaked key lets someone else upload as you until it is reset.

Wire signing into Gradle without leaking passwords

Never write passwords into build.gradle.kts. Put them in a keystore.properties file in the project root:

# keystore.properties (add this file to .gitignore!)
storeFile=/home/you/keys/upload-keystore.jks
storePassword=your-keystore-password
keyAlias=upload
keyPassword=your-key-password

And add these lines to .gitignore right away:

keystore.properties
*.jks
*.keystore

Then load it in app/build.gradle.kts. This version also reads environment variables, so the same file works on a build server later, and someone who clones the project without the keys still gets a working unsigned build instead of an error:

import java.io.FileInputStream
import java.util.Properties

val keystoreProps = Properties().apply {
    val f = rootProject.file("keystore.properties")
    if (f.exists()) FileInputStream(f).use { load(it) }
}
fun signingValue(key: String, env: String): String? =
    System.getenv(env) ?: keystoreProps.getProperty(key)

android {
    signingConfigs {
        create("release") {
            val path = signingValue("storeFile", "RELEASE_STORE_FILE")
            if (path != null) {
                storeFile = file(path)
                storePassword =
                    signingValue("storePassword", "RELEASE_STORE_PASSWORD")
                keyAlias = signingValue("keyAlias", "RELEASE_KEY_ALIAS")
                keyPassword =
                    signingValue("keyPassword", "RELEASE_KEY_PASSWORD")
            }
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            optimization { enable = true }
            // Sign only when keys are available; otherwise build unsigned.
            if (signingValue("storeFile", "RELEASE_STORE_FILE") != null) {
                signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")
            }
        }
    }
}

The book's example comes from a real repository: the author's Flashlight app (chartmann1590/Flashlight) ships a keystore.properties.example with empty values, so anyone who clones the project knows exactly what to provide without anything being exposed.

A bonus rule: versionCode only goes up

Every upload needs a versionCode greater than the one before, and a value can never be reused. That includes builds uploaded to internal tests and builds you later abandon. The author's Dosely app is the book's example: version 1.1.1 had to go out as versionCode 4 because versionCode 3 had already been used by an earlier upload.

The greatest value Google Play allows is 2100000000. Don't jump to a huge number "to be safe" or use a full date-and-time stamp; it can get close to the ceiling quickly. Small, steady increments last forever:

defaultConfig {
    versionCode = 1        // 1, 2, 3 ... one more for every upload
    versionName = "1.0.0"  // major.minor.patch, for humans
}

Checklist before the first upload

  • applicationId is yours, not com.example, and follows the naming rules
  • Upload key created: RSA 2048 or more, valid 25 years or more
  • Keystore stored outside the repo and backed up in two places
  • Passwords in a password manager; keystore.properties and *.jks in .gitignore
  • ./gradlew bundleRelease produces app-release.aab
  • The release variant installed and tested on a real phone (./gradlew installRelease)
  • versionCode increased since the last upload
